ajman/ajman-corniche.programmesIntro: Three routes matter on this stretch: the International GCSE years, the sixth-form fork that follows them, and the Diploma itself for students who take that fork. Each note below is specific to what an Ajman family faces rather than general.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel International GCSE
programmes.description: Linear two-year courses assessed almost entirely by written papers, typically eight or nine subjects. Cambridge tiers many subjects into Core and Extended with different grade ceilings; Pearson Edexcel uses a single tier in most subjects but offers modular entry in some. Science practicals in UAE centres are usually assessed through an alternative-to-practical paper rather than a laboratory examination.
programmes.countryNote: The Corniche decision here is the tier and the board, and both are made by the school. Cambridge runs June and November series with Primary and Lower Secondary Checkpoint tests in March, May and October; Pearson runs May/June and November. Knowing which of those your child is entered for determines the entire revision calendar, and parents are rarely told in those terms.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects at three Higher and three Standard Levels, with Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and Creativity, Activity, Service. Internally assessed components carry roughly a fifth to a quarter of each subject grade and are the only marks banked before the final examinations. The whole qualification is reported as a single total out of 45.
programmes.countryNote: No Diploma campus sits on the Corniche itself; students travel inland to Ajman Academy or across the border to Sharjah. The commute is the reason internal deadlines bite hardest here: the Extended Essay and the subject investigations fall due in the same fortnights as mock examinations, with fewer free evenings to absorb a weak draft.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson International A Level
programmes.description: Three or four subjects studied in depth, assessed by written papers at AS and A2 stages. Cambridge runs the same June and November series as its International GCSE, and every centre is allocated to one of six administrative zones with its own timetable version. Subject combinations are narrower than the Diploma and the written load is lower.
programmes.countryNote: For an Ajman family this is the cheaper and more flexible of the two sixth-form routes, and it is often the right one. It also carries an equivalency consequence worth knowing early: the Ministry's British-track requirement asks for one accredited subject at Advanced Level at grade E or above, or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level, alongside the five International GCSE subjects.

ajman/ajman-corniche.subjectsIntro: These are the subjects Ajman Corniche households book most often. The notes name what is assessed and where the marks tend to go, because 'a maths tutor' and 'Cambridge 0580 Extended tier' are different requests with different answers.

subjects.name: Mathematics (Cambridge 0580 / Pearson 4MA1)
subjects.description: Extended and Higher tier papers hand out method marks generously and students throw them away by not writing the steps. Rounding too early and dropping units account for a steady slice of lost marks at every grade. The tier the school entered the child for sets the ceiling before any teaching happens.

subjects.name: Chemistry (Cambridge 0620 / Pearson 4CH1)
subjects.description: Moles arithmetic and organic pathways decide the top grades. A student who can define a term and cannot explain a trend is being caught by command words rather than by chemistry: 'state' and 'explain' carry different mark allocations and expect different answers.

subjects.name: Economics (Cambridge 0455 / IB DP)
subjects.description: Diagrams earn marks only when labelled and referenced in the prose. The common failure on both routes is accurate theory written with no reference to the named context in the question, which is why a well-informed student can sit stubbornly at a middling grade.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.levels: IB DP HL and SL, IGCSE Business
subjects.description: Application to the given case is the whole assessment. Students who revise concepts and never practise applying them to an unfamiliar organisation lose the application and evaluation marks, which together outweigh the knowledge marks.

subjects.name: Physics (Cambridge 0625 / Pearson 4PH1)
subjects.description: Electricity and waves concentrate the lost marks, usually because circuit reasoning has been memorised rather than derived. The alternative-to-practical paper asks for a method and a control variable, which is a writing task inside a physics paper.

subjects.name: Biology (Cambridge 0610 / Pearson 4BI1)
subjects.description: Volume rather than difficulty is the problem. Transport, homeostasis and inheritance reward exact terminology, and an approximately correct biology answer earns nothing where an approximately correct maths answer might still earn method.

subjects.name: Arabic as a First Language
subjects.description: A full language and literature subject taught in Standard Arabic, with grammar and comprehension demands that do not resemble the additional-language course. KHDA's published Dubai guidance requires separate classes for Arab and non-Arab students, and the federal subject requirement applies in Ajman too.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches / Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Analysis and Approaches carries the algebra and calculus; Applications and Interpretation carries modelling and statistics with a graphical calculator throughout. Engineering and most physics degrees expect the former, and a switch after the first term of Year 12 is costly.

subjects.name: English Language and Literature
subjects.levels: IB DP HL and SL, Cambridge 0500
subjects.description: Unseen text analysis and directed writing in the International GCSE; the Individual Oral and Paper 1 analysis in the Diploma. Students lose marks for retelling rather than analysing, and for structural choices going unmentioned entirely.

ajman/ajman-corniche.regionsTitle: The Corniche and the districts behind it
ajman/ajman-corniche.regionsIntro: Enquiries on this stretch come from a narrow band of seafront towers and the older blocks immediately inland. These are the neighbouring districts whose families ask different questions, and what the difference is.

regions.name: Al Nuaimiya
regions.note: Directly inland and far denser, with larger households in older towers. Enquiries there lean towards catch-up and written-English work rather than the route decisions that dominate the Corniche.

regions.name: Al Zorah
regions.note: The developed frontage north of the Corniche, with low-rise and waterfront housing. Small cohorts and long drives to any IB campus, so single-subject Diploma support is the usual request.

regions.name: Al Rashidiya, Ajman
regions.note: Older residential blocks behind the Corniche with a heavy Indian-curriculum catchment. The common question is the Year 9 move into Cambridge International GCSE and which English qualification follows.

regions.name: Al Jurf
regions.note: Inland and industrial in part, with shift-working households. Lesson slots move week to week here more than anywhere else in the emirate, which online delivery handles better than a visiting schedule would.

regions.name: Al Rawda
regions.note: Villa and townhouse streets where the typical enquiry is a Diploma student choosing three Higher Levels. Study space is not the constraint; subject availability is.

regions.name: Al Mowaihat and Al Zahya
regions.note: The Emirates Road belt, nearest to the IB campuses in the emirate. Middle Years Programme enquiries concentrate here, and the shorter school run means earlier slots are realistic.

regions.name: Emirates City
regions.note: High-rise clusters on the emirate edge with long journeys in every direction. Families here ask about scheduling before they ask about subject, because travel is the binding constraint.

schoolClusters.city: Ajman campuses within reach of the Corniche
schoolClusters.note: The schools nearest the seafront are British and Indian curriculum, with Cambridge and Pearson entries made by the school as an examination centre. A Corniche household often has one child in an Ajman school and a sibling commuting to Sharjah for sixth form.

The tutor sends a short written note after each session recording what was covered and what is set before the next one, which also gives a parent something to check against.

sections.heading: What an Ajman Corniche search is asking, and the answer that has to come first
paragraphs: Before anything else: lessons are delivered one-to-one over live video, and IB Gram does not send a tutor to a Corniche address. Home visits are an India-only service. Saying that first is not modesty, it is the thing a parent needs to know before reading on, and too many pages in this market leave it until the enquiry form.

What follows from it is more interesting than the limitation. The seafront towers sit about twenty-five minutes from Sharjah's school corridor and an hour or more from Dubai's in afternoon traffic. A visiting tutor serving this stretch is drawing from whoever lives within that radius and is paid for the drive either way. A tutor over video is drawn from a pool defined by subject and level, and the lesson starts at the minute it was booked rather than when the car arrives.

The practical test is the subject. For primary number work or Year 8 English, a competent local tutor and a specialist are close to interchangeable, and the person in the room may well win. For Cambridge 0580 Extended tier taught to a child who needs the method marks explained, or for Higher Level Chemistry in a cohort of five, they are not interchangeable at all. The Corniche enquiries skew towards the second kind, which is why this page spends its length on syllabus detail and deadlines rather than on reassurance. It is also why the first question we ask is for the statement of entry rather than for a description of the problem: the entry details answer half of what a Corniche parent is trying to work out, and they take thirty seconds to photograph.

sections.heading: Who lives along the Corniche, and the four decisions that bring parents here
paragraphs: Four household shapes account for most of the enquiries, and each arrives with a different decision rather than a different complaint. Knowing which one you are in shortens the conversation considerably, because the useful answer for a family choosing a sixth-form route has almost nothing in common with the useful answer for a family deciding whether to accept a Core entry.

The smaller household with one or two children is the most common shape here, and the enquiry usually concerns a single subject in depth rather than general support. The second shape is the family whose child is in a small cohort for an unusual subject. The third is the family weighing A Levels against the Diploma, which is a decision made in Year 11 and regretted in Year 12 if it is made on reputation rather than on the child's actual subject profile.

The fourth is the family holding a disappointing result and asking whether a November resit is worth it. That is a genuinely difficult question with a real answer, and it turns on how far below the target the grade fell, which paper lost the marks, and whether the student will be sitting a resit in the same months as the next qualification's coursework. The table below sets the four shapes against the decision each one is actually making, and against the single piece of evidence that usually settles it. In every case that evidence is a document the family already has or can obtain in a day: a statement of entry, a marked paper, a published deadline, or the child's own subject profile written out honestly.

sections.heading: Establishing which board your child is actually entered for
paragraphs: Parents are frequently surprised to learn that 'IGCSE' names two different qualifications from two different awarding organisations. Cambridge International and Pearson Edexcel both offer International GCSEs in the same subjects, with different syllabus codes, different paper structures and different tiering rules. A tutor working from the wrong board's past papers wastes the hour politely, and the student notices before the parent does.

The fastest way to find out is the statement of entry the school issues, which carries the awarding body and the syllabus code. Failing that, the front page of any past paper the school has set will say. A Cambridge code is four digits, for example 0580 for Mathematics, 0625 for Physics and 0620 for Chemistry. A Pearson Edexcel International GCSE code starts with a digit and letters, for example 4MA1 for Mathematics and 4PH1 for Physics. Knowing the code is more useful than knowing the subject name.

The differences then matter in specific ways. Cambridge tiers many subjects into Core and Extended, with Core capped at grade C or its numerical equivalent. Pearson Edexcel more often uses a single tier with a Higher paper, and offers modular entry in some subjects, which allows a student to bank a unit early. Cambridge also allocates every centre to one of six administrative zones, each with its own version of the timetable, and warns that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an examination after the wrong zone's timetable was used.

sections.heading: The entry calendar, counted backwards from the paper
paragraphs: No competitor page in this market publishes an examination calendar, which is strange, because the deadlines are the part parents most often miss. The useful way to read a session is backwards from the paper, because almost everything that can go wrong has a date attached months earlier. The Cambridge March 2027 series is the clearest worked example: the examination period runs from 3 February to 4 March 2027, but final entries are due on 27 November 2026, more than two months before the first paper.

Forecast grades for that series are due on 27 February 2027, results reach centres on Cambridge Direct on 13 May and certificates follow in late June. For Pearson Edexcel the pattern is similar in shape: International GCSE examinations run in May/June and November, with the November 2026 final timetable running from late October to 19 November 2026. June 2026 results went to centres on 19 August 2026 and to students on 20 August; November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026.

Two cautions belong with this. Pearson publishes provisional timetables ahead of each series and revises them, so the live official timetable is the only version worth planning around. And we do not publish IB examination or results dates on this page: the IB's own site blocks automated checking, so no date in this project has been confirmed from the IB itself. UAE schools sit the May session; confirm the specific dates with your child's IB coordinator or on ibo.org rather than taking them from any tutoring website, including this one.

sections.heading: After IGCSE: A Levels or the IB Diploma
paragraphs: This is the decision most Corniche families bring in Year 11, and it is usually framed as which qualification is better. That framing is the problem. Neither is better; they suit different students, and the right answer depends on how narrow the child's strengths are and how much written load they can carry alongside three other commitments.

A Levels concentrate: three or four subjects studied deeply, with fewer required components and no compulsory essay of four thousand words. For a student with a clear direction and a weak spread, that depth is an advantage, and the sixth-form options in and around Ajman are wider for A Levels than for the Diploma. The Diploma spreads: six subjects, a research essay, a Theory of Knowledge course and an activity requirement, reported as one total out of 45. For a student with broad competence and good organisation, it opens more doors and is better preparation for an undergraduate workload.

The equivalency consequence is the part that gets missed. The Ministry's British-track requirement, as clarified in July 2026, asks for one accredited subject at Advanced Level with a grade of no less than E, or two accredited subjects at Advanced Subsidiary Level with the same grade, alongside five accredited International GCSE subjects at grade E or 3 or above. Arabic and Islamic education are not counted among those five. For the IB track no points threshold has been published that we have been able to read on an official source, so verify that with the Ministry directly rather than trusting a figure on a tutoring site.

sections.heading: What moves the price of an hour in Ajman
paragraphs: Published UAE rates read in October 2026 run from about AED 45 to 150 an hour for budget online tuition, with EdFlik advertising from AED 45 to 65 and Tutopiya from AED 33 to 52. A qualified subject tutor online sits around AED 150 to 300, with Unitors quoting from AED 150 for International GCSE and from AED 200 for IB. An in-home visit including travel runs AED 180 to 500, on Bestimate's 2026 figures of AED 180 to 350 and independent home tutors at AED 200 to 500. Specialist IB, IGCSE and A-Level work lands at AED 200 to 450 or more, TutorChase quoting AED 270. Premium examiner-led work is quoted as high as AED 650 by BartyED.

Those are other people's published numbers, dated and attributed, and they exist on this page because almost nobody else in this market publishes any. IB Gram's own figure comes with the consultation, after the subject and level are known, and the free trial lesson that precedes it requires no card details and no commitment. What is worth understanding is which variables move a quote, because four of the five are things a parent can influence.

Level moves it most, and scarcity moves it second. Format is third, and the in-home premium is mostly the tutor's unpaid driving being priced in. Session length is fourth: a 90-minute slot usually costs less per minute than a 60-minute one. Proximity to a session is fifth, and it is the one that catches families out, because specialists commit their diaries in September and a February enquiry for a May series is shopping in a thinner market at a higher price.

sections.heading: Ministry of Education equivalency, and the Year 10 decisions that protect it
paragraphs: Equivalency is the process by which the Ministry of Education recognises a school-leaving qualification for use in the UAE, and it is where a subject choice made at fourteen can come back three years later. The British-track rule clarified in July 2026 asks for passes in five accredited subjects in GCSE or International GCSE certificates at a grade of no less than E or grade 3, plus either one accredited subject at Advanced Level at grade E or above or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade.

Two details inside that rule do the damage. The first is that Arabic and Islamic education are not included among the five required subjects, so a student who counts them towards the total can arrive at the Ministry a subject short. One ranking competitor in this market publishes the claim that UAE candidates must take six International GCSE subjects; the sourced figure is five, excluding those two, and a page that gets this wrong sends parents to buy a subject they did not need.

The second is sequencing. The five subjects have to exist on a certificate, which means they have to have been entered, which means the decision sits in Year 10 rather than Year 13. A family that drops a subject in Year 11 for good reasons should count what remains before confirming it. For the American track the Ministry's clarification sets English proficiency at IELTS academic 5, TOEFL iBT 61, or 450 in the SAT reading and writing section, with at least 450 in SAT Mathematics. No IB points threshold has been published that we could read on an official source. IB Gram does not perform or guarantee equivalency; verify your own case with the Ministry or the relevant attestation authority before acting.

sections.heading: Ramadan, exam leave and the Ajman school calendar
paragraphs: The UAE academic year puts two predictable disruptions in the path of any weekly tutoring arrangement, and planning for them is easier than reacting to them. Ramadan shortens the school day and changes the shape of the evening entirely: a 19:00 slot that worked all year becomes the worst possible hour, and a post-Iftar slot works considerably better. Families who move the slot deliberately keep their continuity; families who try to hold the original time usually lose three or four weeks.

Exam leave and study leave are the opposite problem: they create weekday mornings that do not exist for the rest of the year, and they are the most valuable tutoring hours a commuting student will ever have. A Corniche family with a Year 11 or Year 13 candidate should plan to use them rather than treating them as rest. One ninety-minute morning session on a study day is worth more than two tired evening hours.

The third consideration is the summer. Students sitting a November series are revising through a period when the school is closed and no deadlines exist, which makes it the easiest stretch of the year to drift through. Students moving into a new programme in September benefit from a short run of sessions in August on the specific gap they are carrying, rather than general coverage. Both are planning decisions rather than teaching ones, and both are better made in advance of the term than halfway into it.

sections.heading: Feedback, authorship and the operators who blur the line
paragraphs: Every internally assessed IB component and every piece of International GCSE coursework carries the same condition: the submitted work must be the student's own, and the IB requires the supervisor to authenticate it. There is at least one visible operator in this market selling finished Internal Assessments at a published price. A parent reading tutoring pages in Ajman deserves a plain statement of where the line sits, not a vague reassurance.

A tutor can do a great deal on the permitted side of that line. They can teach the published assessment criteria and what each one rewards. They can discuss whether a research question is answerable inside the word count. They can read a draft and say that the method section would not let a reader repeat the experiment, or that an evaluation names a limitation without explaining its effect on the result. They can teach citation and referencing properly, and they can work through analysis the student has already carried out.

What cannot happen is a tutor becoming the author of any part of it. Not a paragraph, not a rewritten conclusion, not a reworded research question typed by someone else. The test we apply after a session is that every sentence in the file is still one the student typed. Discussion, marginal feedback and teaching on the criteria all pass it. Anything that moves a tutor's words into the submitted document does not, and we decline the request when it is made rather than negotiating around it.

process.description: Board, syllabus code, tier or level, and the examination series. The statement of entry carries all four. With them we can match a specialist in a day or two; without them the match is a guess, and the student discovers it in lesson one rather than the parent in the enquiry.

process.title: Take the decision session if the question is a choice
process.description: If what you need is an answer about a tier, a deadline or a sixth-form route rather than teaching, start there. One session, sources named, no obligation to book lessons afterwards. Several Corniche families finish it needing fewer subjects than they expected.

process.title: Use the free trial lesson
process.description: One full lesson in the subject you asked about, with the tutor you would continue with, no card details and no commitment. The written note afterwards records what the tutor found, which is worth having even if you stop there.

process.title: Place the slot where it survives Ramadan and exam leave
process.description: We book around the Ajman school run and plan the Ramadan move in advance rather than when it arrives. Study days and exam-leave mornings are claimed deliberately, because for a commuting student they are the best hours of the year.

process.title: Review against marked work
process.description: Every four to six weeks we look at what changed on actual marked papers rather than on impressions. If the pattern of lost marks has not moved, the approach or the tutor changes rather than the number of hours.

whyPoints.title: Deadlines with their source attached
whyPoints.description: The Cambridge and Pearson dates on this page come from those organisations' own published key-dates documents and are named as such. IB dates are deliberately absent, because the IB's site blocks automated checking and no date here has been confirmed from the IB itself.

whyPoints.title: A specialist for a cohort of five
whyPoints.description: A Corniche student taking an unusual Higher Level subject in a class of four or five has no second explanation available locally. Online matching draws from a pool defined by subject rather than by driving distance, which is exactly the case where it matters.

whyPoints.title: The right board's papers
whyPoints.description: Cambridge 0580 and Pearson 4MA1 are different qualifications with different papers. We read the entry details before matching, so the hour is not spent on the wrong board's past questions.

whyPoints.title: Equivalency explained, not performed
whyPoints.description: This page sets out the sourced British-track and American-track requirements and says plainly that no official IB points figure has been read. IB Gram does not carry out or guarantee equivalency; the Ministry does, and we point you there.

whyPoints.title: Rates you can check
whyPoints.description: Every dirham figure here is another provider's published number, named and dated to October 2026. That gives a parent on the Corniche something real to judge a quote against, ours included.

whyPoints.title: A stated position on assessed work
whyPoints.description: We teach the criteria, read drafts and give feedback. No tutor becomes the author of an Internal Assessment, Extended Essay or coursework, and we turn that request down rather than finding a form of words for it.

faqs.question: Can a tutor come to a tower on Ajman Corniche?
faqs.answer: Not from IB Gram. We do not send tutors to addresses anywhere in the UAE; home visits are a service we offer only in India. Everything here is one-to-one over live video at a fixed weekly slot in Gulf Standard Time. The reason to prefer that on this stretch is availability rather than cost: a Corniche family needing Higher Level Chemistry or an unusual International GCSE subject is choosing from a pool defined by who teaches that syllabus, not by who can reach the Corniche inside half an hour in afternoon traffic.

faqs.question: Where on the school paperwork does it say which awarding body my daughter is entered with?
faqs.answer: The statement of entry the school issues names the awarding body and the syllabus code, and that is the fastest source. Failing that, the front cover of any past paper the school has set will say. Cambridge codes are four digits, such as 0580 for Mathematics or 0625 for Physics. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE codes mix digits and letters, such as 4MA1 or 4PH1. Knowing the code matters more than knowing the subject name, because the papers, the tiering rules and the practical arrangements all differ between the two.

faqs.question: Is a November resit worth taking after a disappointing June result?
faqs.answer: It depends on three things. How far below target the grade fell, because a single grade gap often closes with focused paper practice while a two-grade gap usually needs content work as well. Which paper lost the marks, since a weak paper two is a different repair from a weak alternative-to-practical. And whether the resit term collides with the next qualification's coursework deadlines. Cambridge runs June and November series and Pearson runs May/June and November, so the entry deadline falls months before the paper; check it with the school before deciding.

faqs.question: After IGCSE, should my son take A Levels or the IB Diploma?
faqs.answer: It turns on how narrow his strengths are and how much written load he carries well. A Levels mean three or four subjects in depth with no compulsory research essay, which suits a student with a clear direction and an uneven spread. The Diploma means six subjects, the Extended Essay, Theory of Knowledge and an activity requirement, which suits broad competence and good organisation. Availability matters too: A Level places are easier to find near Ajman, while the Diploma usually means a commute inland or into Sharjah for two years.

faqs.question: Why is the entry deadline months before the exam?
faqs.answer: Because the awarding organisation has to build a timetable, print and distribute papers to centres worldwide, and allocate examiners before the series starts. The Cambridge March 2027 series is the clearest example: the examination period runs 3 February to 4 March 2027, with final entries due on 27 November 2026 and forecast grades on 27 February 2027. That is why a tier change or an added subject becomes expensive or impossible in January. Ask the school for the entry deadline that applies to your child's series, in writing, in the autumn term.

faqs.question: What makes one tutor cost AED 180 an hour and another AED 450?
faqs.answer: Mostly level and scarcity. Published UAE rates in October 2026 put budget online tuition at roughly AED 45 to 150, a qualified subject tutor online at AED 150 to 300, and IB, IGCSE or A-Level specialists at AED 200 to 450 or more, with one provider quoting AED 650 for examiner-led work. Those are other providers' figures. The honest summary is that lower-secondary general support and Higher Level specialist teaching are different markets, and paying specialist rates for Year 8 maths buys very little extra.

faqs.question: Which subjects should we make sure are on the certificate for UAE equivalency?
faqs.answer: On the British track the Ministry's July 2026 clarification asks for five accredited GCSE or International GCSE subjects at grade E or 3 or above, and states that Arabic and Islamic education are not included among those five. Alongside them it asks for one accredited subject at Advanced Level at grade E or above, or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level. The practical consequence is that the five have to be entered in Year 10, not counted in Year 13. Verify your own case with the Ministry; IB Gram does not perform or guarantee equivalency.

faqs.question: Do lessons move to after Iftar during Ramadan?
faqs.answer: Yes, and we recommend planning the move before Ramadan starts rather than when a session is missed. The school day shortens and the useful evening shifts entirely, so a slot that worked all year becomes the worst hour available. Post-Iftar sessions hold well, and so do late-morning slots on days when school finishes early. Families who move the time deliberately keep their continuity through the month; families who try to hold the original slot typically lose three or four sessions and then restart from behind.

faqs.question: My daughter is the only Economics student in her year. Can tutoring replace a class?
faqs.answer: It cannot replace the discussion a larger cohort would have given her, and it is dishonest to claim otherwise. What it can replace is the second explanation, the marked practice and the comparison of answers that a class normally supplies. For Economics specifically that matters, because the marks sit in application and evaluation rather than in knowledge, and those are skills built by writing an answer and having it challenged. A weekly one-to-one slot with a specialist is the closest available substitute, and for a single-student cohort it is usually the only one.

faqs.question: Is it too late to start in February for a May examination series?
faqs.answer: It is late, not too late, and what changes is the realistic goal. Ten to twelve weeks is enough to repair technique on papers the student already roughly knows: method marks, command words, timing and the specific question types that have been losing marks. It is not enough to teach two years of content that was never learned. The first session should be a timed past paper marked against the published scheme, because that tells you which of those two situations you are in before you commit to a block of hours.

faqs.question: Can my child sit IGCSE papers as a private candidate in the UAE?
faqs.answer: Private candidate entry exists, but it is arranged through a centre rather than directly with the board, and not every centre accepts external candidates in every subject. Science subjects with practical components can be the hardest to place. The right sequence is to find a centre in the UAE that will accept the entry, confirm which subjects and syllabus codes it offers, and only then plan the teaching. Ask about the entry deadline at the same time, since for the Cambridge March series it falls in the previous November.

faqs.question: Do you teach Ajman Corniche students who go to school in Sharjah?
faqs.answer: Regularly, and it is one of the commonest patterns on this stretch. The student attends a Sharjah campus, gets home somewhere between 16:30 and 17:30 depending on the corridor, and takes a lesson at 18:30 or 19:00. Because the lesson is delivered over video it does not matter which emirate the school sits in or which regulator inspects it; what matters is the board, the syllabus code and the level. We do check that the tutor has no connection to the child's own school before matching.

faqs.question: How many subjects should we book tutoring in at once?
faqs.answer: Fewer than most families start with. One subject taught well for a term moves a grade; four subjects at one session a week each usually move none, because the student has no time left to do the work that was set. The sensible method is to rank the subjects by the gap between the current and the needed grade, start with the top one or two, and add a third only when the first is holding. If every subject is slipping at once, the problem is often organisation or language rather than four separate content gaps.

faqs.question: What does a tutor do in the first session that a school cannot?
faqs.answer: Spend a whole hour on one student's errors. A class teacher with twenty-five students and a syllabus to finish cannot stop for forty minutes on the specific reason one child drops method marks in multi-step algebra, and should not. A first session normally works through a recent marked paper question by question, separates wrong answers from answers that were nearly right, and produces a short list of what is actually costing marks. That list is the useful output, and it is worth having even if you decide not to continue.

ajman/al-helio.tutorsIntro: The tutors below teach to named syllabus codes and published assessment criteria rather than to subjects in general. Al Helio households most often book Mathematics, Physics and English, and most often for two children at once in different year groups.

intro.heading: In Al Helio the usual question is not what to teach but why the marks are stuck
paragraphs: Al Helio is the inland villa and townhouse belt behind the older centre of Ajman, running through Al Helio 1, 2 and 3 towards Sheikh Ammar Bin Humaid Street and the Emirates Road. The housing is bigger than almost anywhere else in the emirate: family villas with four or five bedrooms, a majlis, and enough space for a child to study without negotiating for the kitchen table. Households are correspondingly larger. Three and four children are normal, and it is common for one family to have a primary pupil, a Year 10 candidate and a sixth-former in the same building.

That shape produces a specific kind of enquiry. Families here rarely ask whether tutoring exists or what it costs in the abstract. They ask why a child who revises for hours is still sitting at a 5, and they ask it about one child while mentioning two others in the same sentence. The space problem that dominates the apartment districts does not exist here. The problem is diagnosis, and after diagnosis it is logistics: three children, three different syllabuses, one working week.

Diagnosis is genuinely the harder part, and it is the part most tutoring never does. A student losing marks because they do not know the content, a student losing marks because they cannot write to a command term, and a student losing marks because they run out of time in paper two all look identical from the outside: a disappointing number on a report. They need three different interventions, and more hours of the same teaching fixes only the first one. The fastest way to tell them apart is to read a marked paper rather than to ask the student how it went.

The second thing an Al Helio family needs is a plan that treats the children separately. Siblings in different year groups should not be on one shared arrangement, however convenient that sounds, because the one who needs least will absorb the hour. Siblings on genuinely identical work can share a slot, and that is worth doing. The distinction is the board, the tier and the series, not the family name, and it is settled in a minute by looking at the entry details.

IB Gram does not send a tutor to an Al Helio villa. Home visits are a service we provide only in India; every UAE lesson is one-to-one over live video, timed to Gulf Standard Time. In a household running three children, that removes the constraint that usually kills a tutoring plan by week six: the plan no longer depends on anyone arriving, and three different specialists can teach three different children on three evenings without a single car journey. Al Helio families also ask where the sessions sit in an Ajman evening that already holds a school run to Sharjah, and that scheduling question is answered here with the timetable rather than with a promise.

ajman/al-helio.programmesIntro: Three programmes cover almost every Al Helio household, often all three at once in the same family. Each note below describes what is assessed and what that means for a parent trying to read a report.

programmes.name: IB Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups across five years, each subject assessed against four criteria lettered A to D and marked out of eight. The four criterion scores are summed and converted to a 1-7 grade using published boundaries, which is why a student can be strong on knowledge and still be reported at a 4 if the analysis and reflection criteria are weak. MYP 5 ends with the Personal Project.
programmes.countryNote: This is the programme Al Helio parents find hardest to read, and reasonably so. A report that says 'Criterion C: 4' tells a parent nothing unless they know that Criterion C in Sciences is processing and evaluating. Most of the stuck-marks enquiries from this district turn out to be a single weak criterion repeated across several subjects, which is one problem rather than four.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel International GCSE
programmes.description: Two linear years assessed almost entirely by written papers, typically across eight or nine subjects. Cambridge tiers many subjects into Core and Extended with different grade ceilings; Pearson Edexcel usually runs a single tier with Foundation and Higher papers. Science practical skills are generally assessed through an alternative-to-practical written paper in UAE centres.
programmes.countryNote: The failure mode here is almost never content. Al Helio students arriving from an Indian-curriculum primary or a Middle Years Programme usually know the material and lose marks on shown method, precise terminology and timing. The tier matters too: a Core entry caps the grade, and a family running three children rarely checks all three statements of entry.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects, three at Higher Level, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and Creativity, Activity, Service. Each subject includes an internally assessed component worth roughly a fifth to a quarter of the grade. The written papers all fall in a single session at the end of the second year, so internal components are the only marks secured before then.
programmes.countryNote: Al Helio Diploma students travel inland or into Sharjah, and the villa households here usually have younger siblings needing attention in the same evenings. The practical consequence is that a Diploma plan has to be ruthless about which two subjects get weekly time, rather than spreading an hour across six.

ajman/al-helio.subjectsIntro: These are the subjects Al Helio families book most, with the specific place each one tends to lose marks. The pattern is what gets diagnosed; the subject is only where it shows up.

subjects.name: Mathematics (Cambridge 0580 / Pearson 4MA1)
subjects.description: Method marks are given for the steps, and students who work in their heads lose them even when the final answer is right. Early rounding and missing units cost a steady few marks per paper at every grade. Confirm the tier before anything else, because Core sets a ceiling no teaching can lift.

subjects.name: Physics (Cambridge 0625 / Pearson 4PH1)
subjects.description: Electricity and waves hold most of the lost marks, generally because circuit behaviour has been memorised as rules rather than derived. The alternative-to-practical paper asks for a method, a control variable and a source of error, which is a structured writing task more than a physics one.

subjects.name: Chemistry (Cambridge 0620 / Pearson 4CH1)
subjects.description: Moles calculations and organic pathways decide the upper grades. A student who can define a term but cannot explain a trend is being caught by command words: 'state', 'describe' and 'explain' carry different mark allocations and expect visibly different answers.

subjects.name: Biology (Cambridge 0610 / Pearson 4BI1)
subjects.description: The difficulty is volume and precision rather than concept. Transport, homeostasis and inheritance reward exact terminology, and a nearly-right biology sentence earns nothing where a nearly-right maths line might still collect method.

subjects.name: English Language and Literature
subjects.levels: Cambridge 0500 and 0510, IB DP HL and SL
subjects.description: Students lose marks by retelling a text rather than analysing it, and by never naming a structural or language choice. In the Diploma the Individual Oral and the unseen analysis both reward a clear line of argument built from evidence rather than coverage of everything noticed.

subjects.name: Sciences at MYP level
subjects.description: Criterion A is knowledge and understanding; B is inquiring and designing; C is processing and evaluating; D is reflecting on the impacts of science. Most Al Helio MYP students are solid on A and lose the grade on C and D, which no amount of extra content revision will change.

subjects.name: Individuals and Societies at MYP level
subjects.description: Criterion B is investigating and Criterion D is thinking critically, and both reward a stated argument supported by selected evidence. Students who write everything they know score lower than students who write less and choose it deliberately.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches / Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Analysis and Approaches is the algebra and calculus route; Applications and Interpretation is modelling and statistics with a graphical calculator used throughout. Engineering and most physics degrees expect the former, and switching after the first term of Year 12 is painful.

subjects.name: Arabic as an Additional Language
subjects.description: A compulsory subject for non-Arab students in UAE private schools, and a separate subject from Arabic as a first language. The sensible goal for most Al Helio families is a secure pass built from vocabulary and structure, without the subject consuming time the examination subjects need.

sections.heading: What an Al Helio parent is usually trying to diagnose
paragraphs: The enquiry from this district almost always arrives as a puzzle rather than a request. The child works. The child is not lazy, not disengaged, not in trouble at school. The child revises, sometimes for hours, and the grade does not move. A parent in that position does not need a tutor yet; they need to know which of four or five quite different problems they are looking at, because each one has a different repair and three of them do not respond to more teaching at all.

Before anything else, the delivery question: lessons are one-to-one over live video, and IB Gram does not send a tutor to an Al Helio address. Home visits are an India-only service. In a villa district with three children in the house, that turns out to be an advantage rather than a concession, because three different subject specialists can teach three different children on three evenings without anybody driving anywhere.

The diagnosis itself needs evidence rather than conversation. A marked paper, with the examiner's or teacher's annotations on it, tells you in ten minutes what a month of asking a teenager how school went will not. The questions that matter are narrow: were the lost marks for wrong answers or for right-ish answers that missed what the mark scheme wanted; were they clustered at the end of the paper, which is a timing problem; were they clustered in one topic, which is a content gap; or were they spread evenly across every question type, which is usually a technique problem.

sections.heading: Who lives in Al Helio, and what running three children at once actually costs
paragraphs: The defining feature of this district is household size. A villa in Al Helio 1 or 2 commonly holds four to six children spread across primary, lower secondary and sixth form, and the parents are running three different curricula, three different report formats and three different sets of deadlines without any of them lining up. The resource that runs out is not money as often as it is adult attention on a weekday evening.

That produces a predictable pattern. The eldest, with the nearest examination, gets the help. The youngest, who is loud about it, gets some. The middle child, who is quietly sliding from a 6 to a 5, gets noticed in Year 10 when the entry has already been made. This is not negligence; it is what happens when one or two adults are dividing a Tuesday evening five ways, and it is the single most useful thing to plan around deliberately.

The honest advice is to rank rather than to spread. Rank the children by the gap between where they are and where they need to be, weighted by how soon it matters, and buy depth for the top one or two rather than an hour each for all of them. An hour a week in one subject taught to a diagnosis moves a grade. Five hours spread across five children moves nothing, because none of them has time left to do the work that was set.

sections.heading: Five ways a capable student loses marks, and which ones tutoring fixes
paragraphs: These five account for most of the stuck grades in this district, and they are distinguishable from a marked paper in about ten minutes. The reason the distinction matters is that only two of them respond to more subject teaching. The other three respond to something narrower and faster, and a family that books a term of general lessons for a timing problem pays for twelve hours to fix something four would have handled.

The content gap is the simplest: marks clustered in one or two topics, with the rest of the paper fine. It is also the least common among students whose parents describe them as hard-working. The technique gap is the commonest: marks spread thinly across every question, two or three at a time, for unshown method, imprecise terminology or an answer that addressed the wrong command word. The timing collapse shows as a strong first half and an empty last third. The transfer failure shows as fluent homework and weak examinations, because the student can do the procedure when told which procedure to use and cannot select it unprompted.

The fifth is reading, and it is the one most often misread as a subject problem. A student who understands the physics and cannot parse a three-clause question stem is losing physics marks for a language reason. The test is whether the student can answer the same question correctly when it is read aloud to them. If they can, no more physics teaching is required; what is required is practice at dismantling question stems, which is quick work and visible within a month.

sections.heading: Command terms: the vocabulary that quietly decides the grade
paragraphs: Both the IB and the Cambridge and Pearson syllabuses publish lists of command terms, and both expect students to treat them as instructions with specific meanings rather than as synonyms for 'write about'. This is the single most common technique failure in the district and the cheapest to fix, because it is vocabulary rather than content. A student who writes a description where the paper asked for an explanation has usually done the harder thinking and will still score two marks out of five.

The pattern is visible on any marked script. Look for answers with a tick for the first point and nothing after it: that is almost always a student who stated the thing and stopped, on a question that wanted a mechanism or a consequence. Look for long answers with few marks: that is a student describing at length on a question that wanted a short comparison. Neither is a knowledge problem, and neither improves by revising the topic again.

The fix is practice with the mark scheme open, which is a slightly uncomfortable exercise because it requires the student to compare their own sentence against the wording the examiner accepted. Done for twenty minutes a week over a term, it moves marks across every subject at once rather than one subject at a time, which is why it is the first thing we work on for a student whose marks are stuck across the board rather than in one place.

sections.heading: Running two or three children on one weekly plan
paragraphs: The logistics are solvable, but only if the plan is written down. The common failure in a multi-child household is not an ineffective tutor; it is a plan that existed in a parent's head, survived three weeks and then collided with a football fixture, a cousin's visit and a school trip. A plan on paper with one slot per child per week, a named subject and a named evening survives those collisions because everyone can see it.

Two principles make the difference. One subject per slot, because a tutor who is asked to cover maths and physics in one hour will cover neither properly and the child will notice. And separate tutors for separate year groups, because the person who is excellent with a Year 12 Higher Level candidate is rarely the right person for a Year 7 who has lost confidence in number work. Those are different skills, and pretending otherwise saves a parent one conversation and costs a term.

The exception is the genuine shared slot. Two children on the same board, the same tier and the same examination series, with a small gap between them, learn well together and the cost per child drops. The condition is strict on purpose: identical entries, both with their own paper in front of them, both on camera. The moment the gap widens the arrangement stops helping the weaker one, and the right response is to split it rather than to persevere.

sections.heading: What support costs when more than one child needs it
paragraphs: Published UAE market rates read in October 2026 put budget online tuition at roughly AED 45 to 150 an hour, with EdFlik quoting from AED 45 to 65 and Tutopiya from AED 33 to 52. A qualified subject tutor online runs about AED 150 to 300, Unitors quoting from AED 150 for International GCSE and AED 200 for IB. In-home one-to-one including travel runs AED 180 to 500, on Bestimate's 2026 range of AED 180 to 350 and independent home tutors at AED 200 to 500. Specialist IB, IGCSE and A-Level work sits at AED 200 to 450 or more, with TutorChase quoting AED 270 and BartyED AED 650 for examiner-led sessions.

Those figures are other providers' published numbers, attributed and dated, which is more than most pages in this market offer. The reason to put them here is that a household supporting two or three children is making a budget decision, and a budget decision made without a reference point tends to be made badly in both directions: either nothing is bought, or four subjects are bought at once and none of them is finished.

The useful arithmetic for an Al Helio family is per term rather than per hour. One subject, one hour a week, twelve weeks is twelve hours, and at mid-market rates that is a known number that can be compared against a school fee or a set of textbooks. Two children on that basis doubles it. Three children at one hour each, in our experience of how these plans actually run, delivers less than two children at one hour each plus the third monitored, because the household runs out of evenings before it runs out of money.

sections.heading: What to ask an Ajman school when there is no published inspection rating
paragraphs: Private schools in Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah are supervised by the federal Ministry of Education rather than by an emirate-level regulator. Dubai has KHDA, Abu Dhabi and Al Ain have ADEK, Sharjah has the Sharjah Private Education Authority, and Ras Al Khaimah has its own Department of Knowledge. Those authorities publish inspection outcomes in their own formats and with their own levels of detail, and Dubai's six-band scale from Outstanding to Very Weak is the one most parents have heard of.

An Ajman parent comparing schools therefore cannot simply look up a rating in the way a Dubai parent can, and should not assume that an absence of a published band means anything about quality. What they can do is ask the school directly for its most recent inspection outcome and for the documents that actually predict a child's experience. Those documents exist in every school and are rarely volunteered.

The questions worth asking are specific. How many students are in the set for the subject my child is taking, and who teaches it. Which awarding body and which syllabus code is each subject entered with. For Cambridge subjects, which administrative zone is the centre in, since Cambridge allocates every centre to one of six zones with its own timetable version and warns it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who use the wrong one. And how are Arabic, Islamic Education and social studies organised, given the federal requirement that private schools teach them alongside their licensed curriculum.

sections.heading: Evidence a parent can check, week by week
paragraphs: A tutoring arrangement that cannot be checked will drift, and in a busy household it will drift unnoticed for a term. The check does not need to be elaborate. It needs to be something a parent can read in two minutes on a weekday evening and compare against the previous week, and it needs to be about marks rather than about effort or attitude.

What we send after each session is a short note recording what was covered, what was set, and one line on what the tutor is watching. That makes the first check trivial: was the set work done, and did the tutor's one line change over four weeks. If the same weakness is being named in week one and week six, the approach is wrong and the right response is to change it rather than to add hours.

The second check is a marked paper every four to six weeks under timed conditions, scored and compared with the previous one on the specific thing being worked on rather than on the total. A student working on timing should be judged on how much of the paper was attempted, not on the grade. A student working on command terms should be judged on the explain-and-evaluate questions. Totals move slowly and discourage everyone; the targeted measure moves first, and it is the honest early signal that the work is landing. A parent who wants to audit all of that needs no subject knowledge at all: the mark, the criterion label and the date are enough to see whether the line is moving.

sections.heading: Where help stops being help, with several children in the house
paragraphs: Every IB internally assessed component and every piece of International GCSE coursework carries the same condition: the submitted work must be the student's own, and the IB requires the supervisor to authenticate it. In a villa with an older sibling at university and a parent who was an engineer, the line gets blurred at the kitchen table long before any tutor is involved, and it is worth being explicit about where it sits.

A tutor can teach the published assessment criteria and what each one rewards. They can discuss whether a research question is answerable in the word count. They can read a draft and say that the method section would not let a reader repeat the procedure, or that an evaluation names a limitation without explaining its effect on the result. They can teach referencing, and they can work through analysis the student has already carried out. All of that is legitimate and useful, and the Personal Project in MYP 5 is assessed on process, which makes this kind of coaching especially valuable there.

What must not happen is anyone other than the student becoming the author of the submitted text. Not a tutor, not an older sibling, not a well-meaning parent with a relevant degree. The test is that every sentence in the file is one the student typed. Discussion, marginal feedback and teaching on the criteria pass that test. A paragraph supplied by someone else does not, and the consequence of a breach falls on the student rather than on whoever helped, which is the reason to be strict about it rather than relaxed.

process.title: Send a marked paper, not a description
process.description: A recent marked script or a criterion-based report tells us in ten minutes what a long conversation will not. Add the school, the board, the syllabus code and the tier or level. Those five things together are what make a diagnosis possible rather than a guess.

process.title: Take the diagnostic session first
process.description: One session that works through the paper question by question and separates wrong answers from nearly-right ones. The output is a written list of what is actually costing marks. Several Al Helio families find it points to one shared weakness across subjects rather than three separate problems.

process.title: Rank the children, do not spread the hours
process.description: We will say plainly which child to start with: the one whose gap between current and needed grade is largest and soonest. An hour a week in one place moves a grade; five hours split five ways moves none, because nobody has time to do the work that was set.

process.title: Use the free trial lesson
process.description: One full lesson in the subject you asked about, with the tutor you would continue with, no card details and no commitment afterwards. The written note that follows records what the tutor found and is worth keeping either way.

process.title: Check the targeted measure, not the total
process.description: Every four to six weeks, a timed paper scored on the specific thing being worked on. A student fixing timing is judged on how much was attempted; one fixing command terms is judged on the explain and evaluate questions. Totals move last.

whyPoints.title: Diagnosis before hours
whyPoints.description: Most stuck grades in this district are a technique, timing or question-reading failure rather than a content gap, and those three need four to eight sessions rather than a term. We identify which one it is from a marked paper before agreeing a block.

whyPoints.title: A separate plan for each child
whyPoints.description: Siblings in different year groups get different tutors and different slots, because the person who suits a Higher Level candidate rarely suits a Year 7 who has lost confidence. Shared slots happen only where board, tier and series genuinely match.

whyPoints.title: No travel to collapse the plan
whyPoints.description: Lessons are one-to-one over live video, so three children can be taught by three specialists on three evenings without a car journey. In a household this size that is usually the difference between a plan that survives the term and one that does not.

whyPoints.title: Criterion-level reading of MYP reports
whyPoints.description: A report that says 'Criterion C: 4' means nothing without knowing what C assesses in that subject. We read the criteria rather than the grade, which is often how one weakness repeated across four subjects gets found.

whyPoints.title: Rates quoted from published sources
whyPoints.description: Every dirham figure here is another provider's published number, named and dated to October 2026, so a parent budgeting for two or three children has something real to compare against.

whyPoints.title: A clear line on assessed work
whyPoints.description: We teach criteria, read drafts and give feedback. Nobody at IB Gram becomes the author of an Internal Assessment, a Personal Project or a piece of coursework, and we say so rather than leaving it ambiguous.

faqs.question: Can we hire a tutor who drives to our villa in Al Helio?
faqs.answer: Not through IB Gram. We do not send tutors to addresses anywhere in the UAE; home visits are a service we provide only in India. All UAE lessons are one-to-one over live video at a fixed weekly slot. In a large household the practical effect is usually positive: three children can be taught by three different subject specialists on three evenings without anyone driving, and the plan does not collapse the first week a car is unavailable. Independent home tutors do work in Ajman, and published UAE rates for in-home visits run roughly AED 180 to 500 an hour including travel.

faqs.question: Three of my children need help at the same time. Where do we start?
faqs.answer: With the child whose gap between the current grade and the needed grade is largest and soonest, which is usually but not always the eldest. Rank them honestly rather than dividing the week evenly. An hour a week in one subject, taught to a specific diagnosis, moves a grade in a term. Five hours spread across five children moves nothing, because none of them has time left to do the work that was set. The middle child who is quietly sliding is the one to check first, because that slide is the one that gets noticed late.

faqs.question: My son revises for hours and his marks do not move. Why?
faqs.answer: Because revision fixes a content gap, and a content gap is the least likely explanation for a hard-working student whose marks are stuck. Far more often it is technique: two or three marks lost on nearly every question for unshown method, imprecise terminology, or an answer that addressed the wrong command word. Look at a marked paper and ask whether the lost marks were for wrong answers or nearly-right ones. If most were nearly right, more hours of revision will keep producing the same result, and the repair is answer-writing practice with a mark scheme open.

faqs.question: What is a command term, and why does it decide the grade?
faqs.answer: A command term is the instruction word at the start of an examination question, and both the IB and the Cambridge and Pearson syllabuses publish lists of them with defined meanings. 'State' wants one precise line. 'Describe' wants a sequence without causes. 'Explain' wants a mechanism. 'Compare' wants both items in the same sentences. 'Evaluate' wants a judgement with reasons on both sides. A student who writes a description where an explanation was asked for has done the harder thinking and will still lose most of the marks, which is why this is the cheapest technique fix available.

faqs.question: Can one tutor teach my children in different year groups?
faqs.answer: It is possible and usually unwise. A tutor who is excellent with a Year 12 Higher Level candidate is rarely the right person for a Year 7 who has lost confidence in number work; those are different skills, not different amounts of the same skill. Separate tutors and separate slots cost the same per hour and work better. The exception is genuinely identical entries: two siblings on the same board, same tier and same examination series, with a small attainment gap, share a slot productively and at a lower cost per child.

faqs.question: What does supporting two children a week cost in dirhams?
faqs.answer: Published UAE rates read in October 2026 put a qualified subject tutor online at roughly AED 150 to 300 an hour, with specialists for IB, IGCSE and A-Level at AED 200 to 450 or more. Those are other providers' figures, not ours. The useful arithmetic is per term: one hour a week for twelve weeks is twelve hours per child, so two children on separate slots is twenty-four hours a term. A shared slot for siblings with identical entries halves that, and a short diagnostic block of six to ten sessions is often enough on its own.

faqs.question: There is no public inspection report for my child's Ajman school. What can I ask for instead?
faqs.answer: Ajman's private schools are supervised by the federal Ministry of Education rather than an emirate-level regulator, so there is no KHDA-style published band to look up, and its absence says nothing about quality. Ask the school for its most recent inspection outcome, and then ask the questions that actually predict your child's experience: how many students are in the set for each subject and who teaches it, which awarding body and syllabus code each subject is entered with, and how Arabic, Islamic Education and social studies are organised alongside the licensed curriculum.

faqs.question: How do I tell whether a lesson is working after four weeks?
faqs.answer: By checking the targeted measure rather than the total. If the work is on timing, measure how much of a timed paper was attempted. If it is on command terms, measure the explain and evaluate questions specifically. Totals move slowly and discourage everyone. The other check is the written note after each session: if the tutor is naming the same weakness in week one and week six, the approach is wrong and should change rather than being topped up with extra hours. Set work not being done is the other early signal worth acting on.

faqs.question: My daughter freezes in timed conditions but is fine on homework. Is that fixable?
faqs.answer: Usually, and faster than most families expect. Fluent homework with weak examinations is normally a transfer problem rather than an anxiety one: the student can carry out a procedure when told which procedure applies, and cannot select it from an unlabelled question. The test is to give mixed-topic questions with no topic heading. If performance drops, interleaved practice is the repair, and six to eight sessions usually shows. Genuine examination anxiety exists too, and it looks different: the work is fine untimed and collapses even on familiar topics under a clock.

faqs.question: Is 90 minutes too long for a Year 8 student?
faqs.answer: Generally yes. Sixty minutes is the sensible ceiling in lower secondary, and for a Year 7 or 8 who has lost confidence, two shorter sessions beat one long one because the useful work happens in the first forty minutes either way. Ninety minutes earns its length in Mathematics and the sciences at Year 10 and above, where a timed paper plus a review of it genuinely needs that block. For primary-age children the right unit is shorter still: fifteen minutes of reading a day does more than an hour a week.

faqs.question: Do you give homework between sessions?
faqs.answer: Yes, and the work set is the part that actually moves the grade. A lesson can diagnose an error and demonstrate the correct method; only practice makes the correct method automatic. The written note after each session records exactly what was set, so a parent can check it without having to interrogate the student. If set work is not being done week after week, we say so rather than continuing, because an hour spent re-teaching the same point is an hour nobody should be paying for.

faqs.question: My eldest helps the younger ones with maths. Does that count as tutoring?
faqs.answer: For the purposes of the law it may well. The UAE private tuition work permit, introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and issued through MoHRE, is granted free of charge for two years, and the eligible categories include university students and school students aged fifteen to eighteen. That is written for exactly this situation. Unpaid help between siblings in one household is a different matter from paid tutoring, but anyone taking money for private lessons needs the permit, and those without one are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws.

faqs.question: Where does help with a Personal Project stop being help?
faqs.answer: At authorship. The Personal Project in MYP 5 is assessed on process rather than on the finished object, which makes coaching genuinely valuable: a tutor can teach the criteria, question whether the goal is achievable, read the process journal and point out that a reflection records what happened without evaluating it. What cannot happen is anyone else writing the text or making the product. The test is that every sentence in the submitted file is one the student typed. The IB requires the supervisor to authenticate the work, and a breach falls on the student.

faqs.question: What if one child needs a tutor and another needs something else entirely?
faqs.answer: Then we say so. Some of what gets brought to us is not a tutoring problem: a reading difficulty that needs a specialist assessment, an organisation problem that needs a system rather than a subject teacher, or a subject entry that was simply wrong and should be challenged with the school. Booking lessons for any of those wastes a term and money. The diagnostic session exists partly to separate these, and when the answer is that tutoring is not the right purchase, that is the answer you will get.

ajman/al-helio.closingHeading: One marked paper, one child, one subject to start
ajman/al-helio.closingBody: If you are running three or four children in an Al Helio villa and one of them has marks that will not move, the first step is not booking hours for everyone. Send one recent marked paper for the child whose gap matters most, with the board, the syllabus code and the level. intro.heading: Al Jurf is three neighbourhoods wearing one name
paragraphs: Al Jurf is not one place. Al Jurf 1, 2 and 3 are residential streets of villas and mid-rise blocks. Ajman Industrial Area 1 and 2 sit alongside them with warehousing, workshops and the staff accommodation that goes with them. Ajman University occupies the third corner, bringing undergraduates, faculty families and a rental market that turns over every September. A page written for a Dubai villa community describes none of this, and the differences are not cosmetic: they decide what hour a lesson can start and who is in the room when it does.

What those three overlapping populations share is a timetable that does not look like a school's. A parent on a rotating shift in the industrial belt is awake at odd hours and asleep at others. A faculty family keeps university terms rather than school ones. A villa household on Sheikh Ammar Bin Humaid Street runs the school bus at 6.50am and gets a child back at about 4pm. Fixing one weekly tuition slot across that spread is the first practical problem in this district, and it is the reason a rota-friendly online booking beats a visiting tutor who has exactly one free evening.

The academic pressure point is different again. Al Jurf's children overwhelmingly sit Cambridge or Pearson International GCSE, and the decision that shapes their results was taken in Year 10 by somebody else: Core or Extended, Foundation or Higher. That entry sets a grade ceiling. Families rarely see it as a decision at all, because it arrives as information rather than as a question, and by the time a Year 11 works out that the ceiling is binding there is no route back to a higher grade.

The second pressure point is the paperwork at the end. A UAE university will usually want a Ministry of Education equivalency certificate, and the British-track rule counts five accredited subjects at no less than E or grade 3, with Arabic and Islamic education excluded from that count. A child taking nine subjects is fine. A child taking six, two of which are Arabic and Islamic education, is a subject short, and in most cases nobody has mentioned it until the application is being filled in.

So this page is built around tiering, equivalency and the permit question, in that order, with the market's AED rates attached and a straight answer about delivery. Tuition for Al Jurf runs one-to-one online over live video. IB Gram does not send anybody to an Ajman address; home visiting is an India-only service, and the trade is a wider specialist pool in exchange for a screen and a reliable connection.

One more feature of this district matters for planning. A household with an Ajman University student in it often has a ready-made tutor on the sofa, and for Year 8 mathematics that can work perfectly well. It stops working at Higher Level, and it carries a permit question most families have not considered. Both are covered further down, with the resolution number so you can read the rule yourself.
