faqs.question: What am I really looking for when I search for an IGCSE tutor near me?
faqs.answer: Usually four things bundled together. Somebody awake and sharp on Gulf Standard Time at 7.30pm, somebody who understands what an Ajman school report means and which boards local schools enter, somebody responsive who reschedules without a negotiation, and in some cases somebody physically in the room. The first three need no proximity at all. Only the fourth does, and it matters most for younger children and for students who work materially better with a person beside them. Working out which of the four you actually need is the most useful five minutes you can spend.

faqs.question: How far will a tutor realistically travel inside Ajman on a weekday evening?
faqs.answer: Less far than the map suggests, because the relevant number is evening drive time rather than distance. A tutor based in Sharjah faces roughly 15 to 25 minutes to Al Nuaimiya, 30 to 45 to Al Mowaihat or Al Zahya, and 35 to 50 to Emirates City in ordinary evening traffic. For one hour of teaching in Al Mowaihat that is about a three-hour evening commitment. Masfout and Manama are an hour or more each way, which means no weekly in-home arrangement there is rational at any rate anybody would pay.

faqs.question: Is there likely to be an IGCSE tutor within walking distance of Al Rawda?
faqs.answer: For a mainstream subject, possibly. Al Rawda and Al Helio have short internal journeys and an established local pool, so Mathematics 0580 or English 0510 may well be covered within a very short radius. For Additional Mathematics 0606, Computer Science 0478 Paper 2 or the written practical science components, almost certainly not: that pool is small across the whole northern emirates and concentrated towards Dubai. The honest check is to ask any walking-distance candidate for a redacted marked sample from the exact component.

faqs.question: Does a nearby tutor cost less than one based further away?
faqs.answer: For an in-home arrangement, yes, because you are paying for less driving. Published in-home rates of AED 180 to 500 an hour include travel, and the travel share is larger for Al Mowaihat than for Al Nuaimiya. For online delivery the question disappears entirely, since the published AED 150 to 300 band carries no travel component and the tutor's location is irrelevant to the rate. The place a nearby tutor costs you more is choice: a tight radius removes qualified markers from the list and leaves whoever is near.

faqs.question: Are tuition centres in Ajman cheaper than one-to-one tutoring?
faqs.answer: Per hour, almost always, because the cost is shared across a group. Whether they are cheaper per recovered mark depends entirely on the problem. A centre sells a paced scheme of work, which suits a student broadly behind across a whole subject and benefits from a fixed slot and other students in the room. It suits badly a student whose content is in place and who is losing marks on one component, because a group of eight cannot be redirected to one child's error log however good the teacher.

faqs.question: Do tuition centres in Ajman need a licence to operate?
faqs.answer: An operation with premises and staff is regulated differently from an individual tutor, and the instrument depends on the emirate. In Dubai, a training institute requires a KHDA Educational Services Permit, obtained through initial approval followed by a maximum of six months to complete the permit and licence steps, with annual renewal requested at least thirty days before expiry. An individual giving private lessons needs the MoHRE private tuition work permit instead, introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and granted free of charge for two years. Ask any provider which one applies to them.

faqs.question: Why is there no local tutor for Additional Mathematics 0606 in Ajman?
faqs.answer: Because the pool is small nationally and concentrated where the teaching jobs are, which is Dubai and to a lesser extent Sharjah. 0606 is taken by a minority of candidates, so far fewer teachers have ever marked it than have marked 0580, and those who have tend to be attached to schools that offer it. A twenty-minute evening radius around an Ajman address usually contains none of them. A nearby option offered at a routine rate for 0606 is more likely to be someone who has read the syllabus than someone who has marked the papers.

faqs.question: Is a 45-minute IGCSE session worth booking or too short to be useful?
faqs.answer: It is often the best buy for a narrow problem, and it is almost never available locally. An in-home visit carries arrival, settling and departure overheads that make a short booking uneconomic for the tutor and poor value for the family, so the local market sells sixty minutes and upwards. Without travel, a forty-five minute slot with one stated objective becomes viable, and three of them across a fortnight will usually close a recurring unit omission or a misread command word faster and cheaper than one long weekly session covering everything.

faqs.question: Should I pick a tutor who teaches at my child's own school?
faqs.answer: No, and in some emirates it is specifically prohibited. ADEK's professional-ethics rules for Abu Dhabi private and charter school staff prohibit teachers from providing paid private tutoring to students enrolled at their own school, and the code of conduct attached to the MoHRE private tuition permit also bars serving students affiliated with the tutor's own school. That is press-reported rather than read from the current policy text, so verify it if it is material, but the principle holds everywhere. It is a conflict of interest for assessment and predicted grades, and it is not an arrangement to seek out.

faqs.question: What is the cheapest way to get IGCSE help in Ajman this term?
faqs.answer: In order of headline cost: a tuition centre group class, then a budget online tutor at the published AED 45 to 150 band, then a shared session split with another child in the same community, then one-to-one online at AED 150 to 300, then an in-home visit at AED 180 to 500. Cheapest per hour and cheapest per recovered mark are different questions though. For a Year 9 fluency gap the budget band is genuinely right. For a Year 11 component fault it buys somebody who has not marked the paper, which costs more in the end.

faqs.question: Does a nearby tutor understand the Ajman school system any better?
faqs.answer: Not inherently. What matters is whether they know which boards local schools enter, what an Ajman private school report contains, that private schools here sit under Ministry of Education supervision rather than KHDA or SPEA, and that a child enrolled in Sharjah or Dubai gets home materially later. All of that is knowledge rather than proximity. A tutor living three streets away who has never asked for a syllabus code knows less about your child's examination than one in another emirate who asked for it first.

faqs.question: Can I share a local tutor with a neighbour's child to split the cost?
faqs.answer: Yes, and check three things before you do. Both children should be on the same board, the same subject and a similar level, or the session becomes two half-sessions at a discount. The commonest failure in Ajman villa communities is one child entered for Cambridge 0580 and the other for Edexcel 4MA1, where the papers and mark schemes differ enough that neither gets a full hour. Also agree who receives the marked work, because two children need two separate records and shared arrangements tend to produce one vague summary.

faqs.question: What happens if no tutor near Ajman teaches the subject we need?
faqs.answer: You should be told, with a date, before any money changes hands. Thin combinations recur: Additional Mathematics 0606, Computer Science 0478 Paper 2, and the written practical science papers at certain points in the year. The three honest responses are a wait with a named estimate, a related specialist with the limitation stated plainly so you can decide whether the trade is worth it, or a referral elsewhere including to a local provider or a centre. What should not happen is a general tutor presented as a specialist for a component they have never marked.

faqs.question: Is it worth paying more for a Dubai-based tutor than an Ajman one?
faqs.answer: Only if the Dubai tutor has marked the component and the Ajman one has not, and for scarce subjects that is frequently the case. Location itself is worth nothing. Marking experience on the exact paper is worth a great deal, because teaching a subject and training examination technique are different competencies and only the second moves marks on a structured paper. If delivery is over video the question collapses anyway: there is no travel in the rate, so a Dubai-based tutor costs the same as one next door and the choice is made purely on the component.

faqs.question: How quickly can a tutor start if we decide tonight?
faqs.answer: For mainstream subjects, usually within a day or two once we have the syllabus code, the component, the tier and a photograph of the most recent marked script. For the thin combinations it takes longer and you get a date rather than a hopeful wait. The first session is free and is spent marking a question set, so the diagnosis exists after the first hour. What cannot be accelerated is the work: a technique fault needs two to three weeks of marked practice and a content gap needs a term, whatever date you start.

Each one teaches a named syllabus and has marked or taught the exact paper your child will sit, not a general version of the subject.

intro.heading: Start with the inspection report, not the search results
paragraphs: Al Ain is the second city of the Emirate of Abu Dhabi, 130 kilometres inland from the capital and a short drive from the Omani border at Buraimi. That geography decides more about tuition here than most parents expect. The private-school set is far smaller than Abu Dhabi island's, so a Diploma Programme subject is often taught to a single class by a single teacher. If that teacher is strong, your child is fine. If the subject is one the school added recently, there is no second set and no second opinion inside the building.

Because Al Ain falls under the Emirate of Abu Dhabi, its private schools are licensed and inspected by ADEK, the Department of Education and Knowledge, not by KHDA, which covers Dubai, and not by SPEA, which covers Sharjah. This matters practically. ADEK publishes an inspection outcome for each private school it inspects, and the report behind that outcome is written standard by standard: what students achieve, how they are taught and assessed, what the curriculum offers, how they are cared for, and how the school is led. A parent who reads it properly learns which subjects a school is thin in before the mock results arrive.

That is the honest starting point for choosing tuition. An ADEK inspection rating is not a verdict on your child. It is a map of where the school's own capacity sits, and where an outside specialist adds something the school cannot. A school judged strong overall can still have a Physics department that lost two teachers in a year. A school in a lower band can have a Mathematics team that holds its grades. Averages hide subjects, and you are buying support for a subject, not for a school.

IB Gram works the way a good head of year would. You send the last school report and, if you have it, the page of the ADEK report that covers teaching in your child's subject group. We work out whether the gap is content, exam technique, coursework, or the particular habit of answering a command term loosely. Then a tutor who teaches that syllabus takes the student for live one-to-one lessons online. Nothing about that model depends on who happens to live within twenty minutes of Al Mutaredh.

Lessons are delivered online over live video, one tutor to one student, with a shared whiteboard and the student's own past papers on screen. Home visits are a service IB Gram offers only in India. In Al Ain the online format is the better buy and not a compromise: a Chemistry HL tutor who has taught the current guide is worth more than a generalist who can be in Falaj Hazzaa at six. We would rather say that plainly than sell a drive time.

al-ain.programmesIntro: Al Ain families run four routes in practice: the IB continuum through the Primary Years and Middle Years into the Diploma, and the Cambridge or Pearson Edexcel route through IGCSE. Each one is assessed differently, and each one fails differently. Here is what we actually tutor at each stage, and what the Al Ain version of it looks like.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: The PYP has no external exams, which is exactly why gaps go unnoticed until Year 7. Learning is organised around transdisciplinary units and reported against learner-profile attributes rather than percentages, so a child can look settled while number fluency or extended writing quietly falls behind. Tutoring at this stage is diagnostic and short: arithmetic automaticity, reading stamina, and the habit of writing a paragraph that answers the question asked. Thirty focused minutes twice a week does more here than a long session.
programmes.countryNote: In Al Ain, PYP children often move schools when a parent's posting shifts between the city and Abu Dhabi island or Dubai. A move mid-primary usually means a change of curriculum model as well as campus, and the PYP-to-national-curriculum jump exposes gaps in formal grammar and written arithmetic. We start with a short written baseline rather than a conversation, because a Year 5 report that says 'developing' tells a parent almost nothing measurable.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: The MYP marks everything against four criteria per subject on a 1-8 scale, then converts to a 1-7 grade. Students who have never been taught what criterion wording expects tend to plateau at 5 and 6 regardless of ability. Our MYP work is criterion-literal: the student marks their own piece against the published descriptors, sees where the band boundary sits, then redrafts once. eAssessment candidates in Year 11 also need timed practice, which most schools cannot fit inside a lesson.
programmes.countryNote: Al Ain's MYP cohorts are small, and the MYP-to-Diploma step is where the city's limited subject choice bites. A student who wants Physics HL but sat MYP Sciences as an integrated course arrives in DP1 without the algebra load the course assumes. We bridge that in the summer term of Year 11 rather than in October of DP1, when the Internal Assessment clock has already started running.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects, three at Higher Level, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS. The Diploma is scored out of 45, with up to three points from the TOK and EE combination. Most of the pressure is not the final papers; it is the overlap of five Internal Assessments, an Extended Essay and a TOK essay inside the same twelve weeks. Tutoring that ignores that calendar is tutoring for the wrong problem. An IB Diploma tutor in Al Ain should be able to say what is due in week six.
programmes.countryNote: Because few Al Ain schools run every Higher Level science, families here are the most likely in the emirate to need a subject their campus teaches to a handful of students, or does not teach at all. That is the single clearest case for an online specialist: the student gets the Chemistry HL tutor who has taught the current guide, from wherever that tutor is, rather than the nearest adult who did Chemistry at university a decade ago.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel IGCSE
programmes.description: IGCSE is code-specific, and the code changes what you revise. Cambridge IGCSE 0580 Mathematics tiers into Core and Extended, with Extended targeting the upper grades; 0625 Physics, 0620 Chemistry and 0610 Biology carry an alternative-to-practical or practical paper depending on the school's entry. Pearson Edexcel runs 4MA1 for Mathematics A and 4PH1, 4CH1 and 4BI1 for the sciences, with its own January series. We teach to the code on the student's statement of entry, not to a generic IGCSE.
programmes.countryNote: IGCSE tuition in Al Ain is complicated by mixed entries: it is common for one family's two children to sit Cambridge at one school and Edexcel at another, and for a single student to carry both boards across subjects. Before the first session we ask for the statement of entry and check the tier, the board and the practical arrangement. Half the wasted revision we see in this city is a student working through the wrong board's past papers.

al-ain.subjectsIntro: These are the Diploma Programme subjects Al Ain families request most, with what each one is actually assessed on. Where a subject is taught to one small class in the city, an online specialist is usually the only way to get someone who has taught the current guide rather than the previous one.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Under the current guide both levels are assessed on Paper 1 at 36 per cent, Paper 2 at 44 per cent and the scientific investigation at 20 per cent. Marks go missing in the data-based section of Paper 1B and in extended reasoning about energetics and equilibrium. A Chemistry HL tutor works from the student's own marked Paper 2 rather than from a textbook chapter.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: The same 36/44/20 split applies. The HL-only material in fields, induction and quantum physics tends to arrive late in DP2, which is why Al Ain students often meet it for the first time three weeks before a mock. Sessions focus on unit discipline, graph linearisation and the difference between a derivation and an explanation in a six-mark answer.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Biology rewards precision of language more than any other DP science: a correct idea in loose wording scores nothing. We drill command terms against the published markscheme, then work on the long-answer questions in Paper 2 where students lose marks for describing a process when the question asked them to explain or to compare.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: SL is Paper 1 at 40 per cent, Paper 2 at 40 per cent and the exploration at 20 per cent. HL adds Paper 3, worth 20 per cent, with two extended investigative questions that reward stamina and structure. Non-calculator fluency on Paper 1 is the usual weak point for students who learned maths on a graphical display calculator.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: AI is not the easy route; it is the modelling and statistics route, with heavy technology use and a different Paper 3 at Higher Level. Students who chose AI for the wrong reason struggle with the volume of interpretation writing. We also check the route against degree plans, because some engineering and physics programmes still expect Analysis and Approaches.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: SL splits 40/40/20 across Paper 1, Paper 2 and the portfolio of three commentaries. HL moves to 20/30/30/20 and adds the quantitative Paper 3, which is where HL grades are won and lost. Diagram accuracy and the explicit use of the nine key concepts carry marks that students regularly leave on the table.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: The business research project at HL and the written commentary at SL are coursework pieces that need a real organisation and a real question, which is harder in a smaller city. Exam marks are lost on tool-dropping: naming SWOT or Ansoff without applying it to the stimulus. We work from the published assessment criteria outwards.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: SL is Paper 1 at 35 per cent, Paper 2 at 35 per cent and the individual oral at 30 per cent. HL replaces part of that with the HL essay of 1,200 to 1,500 words and reweights the oral. The guided analysis in Paper 1 is a timed close-reading skill, and it is teachable in a way that reading more books is not.

subjects.name: Arabic A and Arabic B
subjects.description: Arabic runs two different ways in Al Ain: as a first language and literature course, and as a second language at B or ab initio level. Both are assessed on productive skills, and both reward structured writing practice far more than vocabulary lists. This is one of the subjects a smaller school set struggles to staff at Higher Level.

subjects.name: Computer Science
subjects.description: The internal assessment is a working solution with documented development, and students regularly build something impressive that documents poorly. We split the work: design and testing evidence first, code second. Paper questions on data structures and object-oriented design need pencil-and-paper tracing practice, not more time in an IDE.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge and the Extended Essay
subjects.description: The TOK essay answers one of six prescribed titles in 1,600 words and is marked out of 10 on a single global impression; the exhibition adds three objects and 950 words. The Extended Essay is 4,000 words, marked out of 34. Together they carry up to three Diploma points. Tutors coach structure, argument and source handling only.

al-ain.igcseSubjectsIntro: On the IGCSE side the board and the syllabus code decide the revision plan. These are the subjects Al Ain parents ask about most often, with the codes you will find on the statement of entry.

igcseSubjects.name: Mathematics
igcseSubjects.description: Cambridge IGCSE 0580 tiers, and a student entered for Core cannot reach the top grades however well they revise, so the tier decision matters more than any single topic. Edexcel 4MA1 is untiered at Higher and sets longer multi-step questions. Both reward method marks, which students lose by not writing the working down.

igcseSubjects.name: Physics
igcseSubjects.description: Electricity and the equations around it account for a large share of lost marks every series. Circuit reasoning, not formula recall, is the skill. Where a school enters students for the alternative-to-practical paper, we drill apparatus description, anomalous-result spotting and table-and-graph conventions on screen using past practical papers.

igcseSubjects.name: Chemistry
igcseSubjects.description: Moles calculations and organic reaction pathways are the two reliable separators at grade 7 and above. We also work on qualitative analysis questions, which read as recall but are really a sequence: observation, deduction, ionic equation. Students who skip the middle step lose both marks.

igcseSubjects.name: Biology
igcseSubjects.description: The content is large and the examiner's vocabulary is narrow. Sessions pair a topic sweep with markscheme language drills on transport, homeostasis and inheritance. Genetic-cross questions are worth practising until the Punnett square layout is automatic, because presentation itself carries marks.

igcseSubjects.name: Economics and Business Studies
igcseSubjects.description: Both subjects are marked on application to the case material, not on definitions. The common failure is a correct textbook answer that never touches the business in the extract. We teach the two-mark, four-mark and extended-response shapes separately, because they are different writing tasks.

igcseSubjects.name: English
igcseSubjects.description: First Language English and English as a Second Language are different examinations with different reading demands, and students are occasionally entered for the one that suits the school rather than the student. Directed writing and summary tasks are the most coachable components in the whole IGCSE set.

al-ain.regionsTitle: Al Ain districts we schedule around
al-ain.regionsIntro: Al Ain is low-rise and spread out, and the school run shapes the timetable more than traffic does. These are the districts families book from most, with the scheduling detail that matters when you are fixing a weekly slot in Gulf Standard Time.

regions.name: Asharej
regions.note: The district next to the United Arab Emirates University campus, so households here often include a parent or sibling on the UAEU timetable. Study-space competition at home is real; we book sessions when the room is quiet, often after 7pm, rather than straight after school.

regions.name: Al Jimi
regions.note: Dense, central and close to Al Jimi Mall, with several of the city's long-established private schools within a few minutes' drive. Pick-up is quick here, so a 4.30pm or 5pm start is realistic even in exam term, which makes Al Jimi families the easiest to give a consistent weekday slot.

regions.name: Al Mutaredh
regions.note: Villa district close to the oasis and the central hospital, with a high share of medical and university households. DP sciences and maths dominate requests from here. Evening sessions work well because parents on shift patterns prefer a fixed slot the student can keep without a lift.

regions.name: Al Muwaiji
regions.note: West of the centre, near the Al Ain Palace Museum side of town, and a longer run back from the newer campuses on the city's edge. A 5.30pm start is safer than a 4.30pm one here; we build the first session late and bring it forward once the family sees the real arrival time.

regions.name: Al Towayya
regions.note: Established residential area with a mix of British and Indian curriculum families, which means one household often runs IGCSE and CBSE timetables side by side. Siblings are better scheduled back to back on the same evening so one quiet room covers both lessons.

regions.name: Zakher
regions.note: On the southern edge towards Jebel Hafeet, with the longest school commute in the city for families whose children attend central campuses. Weekday sessions realistically start at 6pm. Many Zakher families move their heavier work to Friday or Saturday mornings instead.

regions.name: Falaj Hazzaa
regions.note: Large villa neighbourhood with a strong Emirati household share, so Arabic as a first language and Islamic Education sit alongside IB or IGCSE subjects in the same week. We coordinate so tuition does not collide with the school's own Arabic support sessions.

regions.name: Hili and Al Foah
regions.note: Northern districts out towards the Omani border crossing, where the archaeological parks are. Families here drive further for school than anyone else in Al Ain, and the online format removes the second journey entirely. Winter sunset timings change what counts as a late slot.

schoolClusters.city: Central Al Ain: Al Jimi, Al Mutaredh and Al Towayya
schoolClusters.note: The city's oldest private-school cluster, mostly British and Indian curriculum, feeding Cambridge and Edexcel IGCSE entries with A-level or Diploma continuation depending on the campus. Requests from this cluster skew to IGCSE sciences in Year 11 and to DP maths in Year 12.
schools: Our Own English High School, Al Ain
Al Dhafra Private Schools, Al Ain
The International School of Choueifat, Al Ain

schoolClusters.city: Outer Al Ain: Asharej, Zakher and the Abu Dhabi road side
schoolClusters.note: Newer and larger campuses on the city's edges, with the longest commutes and the broadest subject offer. This is where Higher Level science cohorts are smallest, and where a family is most likely to need a subject the campus runs for a single group.
schools: Al Ittihad National Private School, Al Ain

schoolClusters.city: Al Ain students sitting exams outside the city
schoolClusters.note: Some families keep a child at an Abu Dhabi island or Dubai school through a posting, or enter a private candidate through an examination centre elsewhere in the emirate. Online lessons continue through both situations without a change of tutor, which is the practical argument for the format.

al-ain.schoolDisclaimer: Schools are named here as local context only, and no affiliation, endorsement or partnership is implied. Curricula, exam boards and inspection outcomes change from year to year, so confirm the current position with the school and with ADEK before making a decision.
al-ain.modesIntro: Three formats cover almost every Al Ain request. All of them are live one-to-one video lessons with a shared whiteboard, and all of them are timed in Gulf Standard Time. The choice is about rhythm, not about delivery.

modes.title: Weekly one-to-one through the term
modes.description: One or two fixed sessions a week against the school's own scheme of work, which is the format that actually changes a grade over a year. The tutor sees the marked class assessments, so the session targets the question the student got wrong last week rather than the next topic in the book. Most Al Ain families start here with a single subject and add a second only if the first is holding.
bullets: A fixed weekday slot the student keeps without needing a lift
Session plan driven by the school's marked work, not a generic scheme
Written note to the parent after every second session
Siblings scheduled back to back so one quiet room serves both

modes.title: Coursework clinics for the IA, EE and TOK essay
modes.description: Short, scheduled blocks aimed at one assessed piece, pinned to the school's internal deadline rather than the final submission date. The tutor reads the draft against the published criteria, marks it in the student's presence, and names the criterion losing the marks. The student does the rewriting. This is IA coaching, not drafting, and the boundary is explained to the student in the first session.

Research question narrowed before any writing begins

modes.title: Exam-term intensives counted back from the paper
modes.description: Blocks of three to eight sessions built backwards from the first paper of the May or November session, or from the Cambridge and Edexcel series dates. Content revision stops early; the last fortnight is timed papers marked against the official markscheme. During Ramadan these move to post-Iftar sessions, which for many Al Ain students is the most productive slot of the day anyway.

sections.heading: What an ADEK rating actually says about your child's subject
paragraphs: ADEK licenses and inspects the private schools of Abu Dhabi, Al Ain and Al Dhafra, and publishes an overall outcome for each school it inspects on a six-band scale running from Outstanding down to Very Weak. Those words are the part parents remember. They are also the part that tells you least, because an overall band is a weighted summary of an entire school across every phase and subject group it offers.

The useful information sits one level down. An inspection judgement is built from performance standards covering what students achieve, their personal development, teaching and assessment, the curriculum, the care and support around them, and leadership. Achievement itself is reported by phase and by subject group, which is where a parent of a DP2 Chemistry student should be reading. A school can hold a strong overall band while the judgement on attainment in secondary science sits a band lower, and that gap is the one tuition is for.

So use the band for what it is good at. It tells you the direction the school is moving and how much slack the leadership has. A school that has just moved up a band is usually investing in teaching and may fix your problem by itself within a term. A school holding a lower band for several cycles is unlikely to solve a single subject's staffing in the twelve weeks before your child's mocks, and that is a decision point rather than a complaint.

The table below is how we read each band when a family in Al Ain asks what it means for them. It is a working interpretation, not an official definition, and the current report for any named school should be checked on ADEK's own site before you act on it.

sections.heading: The six things an inspector looked at, and which of them you can fix privately
paragraphs: An inspection report is not a review. It is a structured judgement against standards, and each standard has a different relationship to private tuition. Two of them a tutor can genuinely compensate for. Two a tutor can partly offset. Two are entirely the school's, and no amount of tuition will touch them. Knowing which is which stops families spending money on the wrong problem.

Students' achievement, meaning attainment and progress against curriculum standards, is the standard tuition addresses directly. Teaching and assessment is the second: where a report says feedback is not used well to move learning on, an outside tutor marking the student's own work to the published markscheme is a direct substitute for the missing feedback loop. Those two are the reason most Al Ain families start.

Curriculum, and the care, guidance and support standard, are partly addressable. If the report notes that the curriculum is not adapted for higher attainers, a tutor can extend a student beyond the class pace. If it notes weak transition support between MYP and DP, a bridging block in the summer term covers much of it. What a tutor cannot replace is subject choice: if the school does not run Physics HL, tuition does not create a class, although it does make a private or transferred entry survivable.

Personal and social development, and leadership and management, are the school's own. A tutor has no standing there, and any provider implying otherwise is selling something it does not have. We say this openly because it narrows the question usefully. Read the achievement and teaching judgements for your child's phase, decide whether the gap is content or technique or feedback, and buy exactly that.
bullets: Directly fixable by tuition: attainment, progress, exam technique, marked feedback
Partly offsettable: curriculum stretch, transition between programmes, coursework guidance
Not fixable from outside: subject availability, pastoral provision, school leadership
Always read the achievement judgement for your child's phase, not the overall band

sections.heading: What tuition costs in Al Ain, and who publishes those numbers
paragraphs: Published pricing in this market is scarce, and that is deliberate on most sites. Three of the larger agencies competing for UAE search traffic publish no hourly figure at all, and two of those that do quote in US dollars, a currency no family here transacts in. Two more publish a rate in their structured data that contradicts the rate on the visible page. So before anything else: the figures below are market rates other providers publish, not IB Gram's price list.

The pattern across the market is consistent once you convert everything into dirhams per hour. Budget online tuition, usually delivered by university students, starts in the AED 45 to 150 band. A qualified subject tutor working online sits roughly between AED 150 and AED 300. Visiting in-home tuition carries its travel cost inside the hourly rate and runs higher, commonly quoted between AED 180 and AED 500. Named IB and IGCSE specialists sit from AED 200 to AED 450 and above, and examiner-level or heavily branded tutors are quoted at AED 500 to AED 650 and beyond.

Monthly packaging is where comparison gets slippery. Advertised bundles in the UAE include around AED 799 a month for eight online sessions and roughly AED 1,599 to AED 1,799 a month for four two-hour in-home visits. Those are not comparable products: one buys eight contact hours, the other eight hours with travel folded in and half the frequency. Work in cost per contact hour and the picture clears up immediately.

Al Ain sits at the softer end of in-home pricing compared with Dubai, simply because the driving is easier and the rent lower, but the tutor pool is correspondingly smaller. That is the real trade-off for home tuition rates in Al Ain: you may pay less per hour than a Dubai Marina family and still have a much shorter list of people who have taught your child's actual syllabus.

sections.heading: In-home tuition in Al Ain against live online one-to-one
paragraphs: Parents searching for a home tutor in this city are asking a reasonable question, and it deserves a straight answer rather than a redirect. In-home tuition does real things that online does not. A tutor in the room can see a child's body language, put a hand near the page, and keep a distractible twelve-year-old on task without a single reminder. For younger children and for students with certain additional needs, that presence is worth paying for, and families should weigh it honestly.

What it costs is the other half of the answer. An in-home session in Al Ain pays for the tutor's road time, and because the city is spread out from Zakher in the south to Hili in the north, one visit can absorb forty minutes of driving at each end. That time is in the rate, and it also caps the tutor's availability: whoever teaches your child on Tuesday at five must be physically within reach of your district on Tuesday at five. In a city with a small specialist pool, that constraint, not the money, is what usually decides the match.

IB Gram delivers tuition for UAE families as live one-to-one lessons online, over video, with a shared whiteboard and screen sharing. Home visits are part of our India service only. We are not pretending that online is identical to a tutor in the room; we are saying that for Diploma and IGCSE students the specialist you reach matters more than the metre of distance, and that the saved travel converts into frequency and continuity. A student who keeps the same tutor through a house move, a posting to Abu Dhabi island, or a summer abroad does not lose a term to re-matching.

sections.heading: The exam calendar, counted backwards from the first paper
paragraphs: Almost no competitor page in this market names an exam session at all, which is strange, because the session date is the only fixed point in the whole year. Everything else, including how much tuition is worth buying, follows from it. The Diploma runs two sessions: May, which is what nearly all Al Ain schools enter, and November. Cambridge IGCSE runs a May or June series and an October or November series. Pearson Edexcel adds a January series for many International GCSE subjects, which is why a January entry quietly exists in this city for resitting students.

Work backwards and the year has a shape. A year out, the decisions are structural: subject and level combinations, Mathematics AA and AI route choice, and whether a Higher Level science the school cannot staff should be carried. Nine months out, Internal Assessment topics are chosen and approved, and this is where most of the damage is done, because an unworkable research question costs the student weeks they never get back. Six months out, candidate registration has closed and the statement of entry exists; check the board, the tier and the paper options on it rather than assuming.

Three months out, coursework should be finished, and the student should be sitting whole timed papers rather than revising topics. Six weeks out is the point at which new content stops being worth teaching and markscheme behaviour starts paying. In the final fortnight the only useful work is timed questions, marked, with the errors logged by type rather than by topic. Results land in early July for the May Diploma session and in early January for the November session, with Cambridge and Edexcel publishing in August and January; confirm your own dates with the school's exams officer, because entry deadlines vary by centre.

Ramadan moves the middle of this plan. School days shorten, evenings restructure around Iftar, and the productive hours for a teenager shift late. We plan around it rather than through it: lighter content weeks, then post-Iftar sessions for the heavier work.

sections.heading: Where the marks sit: the weightings families misread
paragraphs: A surprising amount of wasted revision in Al Ain comes from not knowing what each component is worth. Parents hear that a paper is hard and buy tuition for it, when the component actually losing the grade is a coursework piece marked months earlier, or a paper that carries nearly half the subject and gets a third of the practice. The weightings are published by the IB for every subject; they are not a secret, they are simply never put in front of parents.

In the current Diploma sciences, both Standard and Higher Level sit at Paper 1 for 36 per cent, Paper 2 for 44 per cent and the scientific investigation for 20 per cent. Read that again: the investigation is worth more than double a strong performance on any single long-answer question, and it is the one component the student controls completely, in their own time, with feedback allowed. A family deciding between coursework support and exam cramming should usually take the coursework first.

Mathematics splits differently by level. At Standard Level, Papers 1 and 2 take 40 per cent each with the exploration at 20 per cent. At Higher Level, Papers 1 and 2 drop to 30 per cent each and Paper 3 takes 20 per cent, which means the HL paper students practise least carries as much as the exploration they agonise over. Economics shifts even harder: Higher Level moves Paper 1 down to 20 per cent and brings in the quantitative Paper 3 at 30 per cent.
The table lists the splits we work from. Weightings are revised between syllabus cycles, so check the current subject guide or ask the school's coordinator before building a plan around them.

sections.heading: The Internal Assessment, criterion by criterion, with the marks attached
paragraphs: No competitor page in this market names a single assessment criterion, which is remarkable given that the Internal Assessment is where a fifth of most Diploma subject grades is decided. The criteria are published by letter with marks attached, and a student who has not read them is marking blind. The first thing we do in IA coaching is put the criteria next to the draft and have the student mark their own work. It is usually an uncomfortable twenty minutes and it saves weeks.

In the current science guides the scientific investigation is marked out of 24 across four criteria of six marks each: research design, data analysis, conclusion and evaluation. The pattern of loss is predictable. Research design loses marks for a vague methodology and an unjustified range of values. Data analysis loses them on uncertainty handling and unlabelled graphs. Conclusion loses them when the student restates results instead of comparing them with accepted values and published literature. Evaluation loses them on generic limitations: writing that there was human error is worth nothing.

The Mathematics exploration is out of 20, split across presentation, mathematical communication, personal engagement, reflection and the use of mathematics, with that last criterion worth 6 marks and depending on the mathematics being commensurate with the level studied. An exploration that uses nothing beyond the first year of the course caps itself regardless of how neat it looks. The Economics portfolio is three commentaries of 800 words each, marked out of 14, with explicit marks for diagrams, terminology, application, a named key concept and evaluation. The Extended Essay is 4,000 words out of 34, and critical thinking alone carries 12 of those marks.
Read those numbers once and the priorities invert. The student who spends a weekend formatting an essay is protecting 4 presentation marks while leaving 12 critical-thinking marks untouched.

sections.heading: What a tutor may and may not do with an IA, EE or TOK essay
paragraphs: This has to be said plainly, because at least one provider selling to UAE families offers completed Internal Assessments at a fixed price. That is not tutoring. Submitting work that is not your own is malpractice under the IB's academic integrity rules, the school is required to act on it, and the consequence falls on the student, not on the person who sold the document. A family paying for that is buying a risk to the whole Diploma.

The honest boundary is easy to describe. A tutor may teach the subject content the coursework rests on, explain what each criterion rewards, discuss the suitability of a research question, show the student how to mark a draft against the descriptors, point out where a paragraph describes instead of argues, and check that referencing meets the school's required style. All of that is ordinary teaching and all of it is allowed.

A tutor may not write, rewrite or redraft any part of the submitted text, supply paragraphs for the student to insert, produce or alter data, choose the research question for the student, write reflection or process-journal entries, or edit a draft line by line until the voice is no longer the student's. The last one is where well-meaning help usually crosses over, and it is also the easiest for a supervisor to spot, because the writing stops matching everything else the student has produced that year.
We tell students this in the first coursework session and we tell parents the same thing. If a provider cannot say where its own line is, that is the answer to the question.

sections.heading: MoE equivalency, UAEU and what an Al Ain leaver needs on file
paragraphs: Al Ain is a university city. The United Arab Emirates University sits in the Asharej area, and a meaningful share of local Diploma and IGCSE students apply to it or to another UAE institution rather than going abroad. That makes one piece of paperwork more important here than in most Gulf cities, and it is one that no competitor page in this market mentions: the Ministry of Education certificate of equivalency.

The principle is straightforward. A UAE university needs to know that a foreign school-leaving qualification is equivalent to the national secondary certificate, and the Ministry issues an equivalency decision on that basis. For an IB student the question is usually whether the full Diploma was awarded rather than a certificate of individual subjects, and whether the subject spread and points total meet the published threshold. For a British-curriculum student it is a count: a required number of IGCSE or GCSE passes alongside a required number of AS or A-level subjects, in a recognised combination. For students required to study Arabic and Islamic Education, those subjects form part of the file.

Where this goes wrong is almost never academic. It is a certificate issued under a previous passport name, a transcript that was never attested, a student who sat a resit at a centre the school did not record, or a family that only discovers at application time that the subject combination does not satisfy the rule. Start the MoE equivalency certificate file in DP1 or Year 11, not in July. Keep the originals, keep every statement of entry, and check the current requirements on the Ministry's own equivalency portal, because the rules are revised and this page is not the authority on them.

UAE University admissions, like other national institutions, also publish their own entry tests and English-language thresholds alongside the equivalency requirement, and those are a separate matter from the Diploma score. Deal with them as a separate deadline, because a student can hold the points and still miss the intake on a language score nobody flagged.

sections.heading: Arabic, Islamic Education and UAE Social Studies alongside the Diploma
paragraphs: Something that is almost completely absent from tutoring pages aimed at UAE families: an IB or IGCSE student in Al Ain is not only studying IB or IGCSE. ADEK requires private schools in the emirate to teach Arabic, Islamic Education for Muslim students, and UAE Social Studies or moral education, in specified amounts and for specified year groups. These sit on top of a six-subject Diploma, and the hours are real.

For Emirati families, particularly in districts such as Falaj Hazzaa and Al Muwaiji where Arabic as a first language is standard, this means the week already contains a demanding literacy load before any Diploma subject is counted. For expatriate families it often means a child studying Arabic as an additional language to a standard the school sets, with marks that appear on the school report but not on the Diploma. Parents are regularly surprised by how much of a term's grade pressure comes from this side of the timetable.

Practically, this changes how we schedule rather than what we teach. Arabic and Islamic Education support sessions a school runs are usually fixed, so tuition goes around them. We ask for the full school timetable, not just the subject in question, before fixing a slot, and we do not book a DP Chemistry session into the one evening a student already has school Arabic support. A tutor who ignores this side of the week ends up competing with it, and the student loses either way.

We also keep the honest limit visible. Where the requirement is a school-set Arabic course rather than an examined IB or IGCSE syllabus, the school's own department sets the standard and the materials, and our role is scheduling around it and supporting study skills, not second-guessing what the school assesses.

process.title: Send the report and the inspection page
process.description: Share the most recent school report, any marked assessment, and if you have it the section of the ADEK report covering teaching and achievement in your child's phase. Twenty minutes of reading replaces an hour of guessing, and it frequently changes which subject we recommend starting with.

process.title: Confirm board, level and entry
process.description: We check the statement of entry or the school's confirmation: Diploma level, or Cambridge and Edexcel codes and tiers for IGCSE, plus the practical arrangement for sciences. This is the step that prevents a term of revision from the wrong board's past papers, which is commoner in Al Ain than anyone admits.

process.title: One diagnostic session on a real paper
process.description: The first session is a marked past paper or a marked piece of coursework, not an introduction. The tutor identifies whether the gap is content, technique, coursework or timing, and tells you which. If the answer is that your child does not need weekly tuition, you will hear that too.

process.title: Fix a slot in Gulf Standard Time
process.description: We set a weekly slot around the school run, the school's own Arabic or Islamic Education support, and sibling timetables. Zakher, Hili and Al Foah families usually land on a later start. Ramadan moves sessions to post-Iftar automatically rather than cancelling them.

process.title: Written feedback the parent can read
process.description: After every second session you receive a short note: what was covered, what the student got wrong, and what changes next. Marked work is annotated on screen and saved where you can open it. No scores are promised, and a session that went badly is reported as a session that went badly.

process.title: Reset before each exam block
process.description: Ahead of mocks and of the May or November session we rebuild the plan backwards from the first paper: the date new content stops, which papers are sat timed, and which error types are being drilled. Blocks end when the exam ends rather than rolling on by default.

whyPoints.title: Matched to the syllabus, not to the district
whyPoints.description: The question is not who can reach Al Towayya by five. It is who has taught the paper your child is sitting, in the current guide, with the markscheme in front of them. Online delivery means the answer to that question is not limited to the people living within driving distance of your street.

whyPoints.title: We read the ADEK report with you
whyPoints.description: Al Ain schools are inspected by ADEK, and the report says more than the headline band. We read the achievement and teaching judgements for your child's phase with you and say which gaps tuition can realistically close and which belong to the school. That conversation is free and sometimes ends in us recommending nothing.

whyPoints.title: A stated line on coursework
whyPoints.description: Tutors teach content, explain criteria and mark drafts. They do not write, redraft or supply any part of an Internal Assessment, Extended Essay or TOK essay, and they do not produce data. The student hears that boundary in the first coursework session, in the same words a supervisor would use.

whyPoints.title: Market pricing shown, not hidden
whyPoints.description: The AED bands on this page are figures other providers publish, attributed to them, so you can see where any quote you receive sits. We do not pretend a monthly bundle and an hourly rate are the same product, and we would rather you compared cost per contact hour than per month.

whyPoints.title: Scheduling that respects the Al Ain week
whyPoints.description: Sessions are booked in Gulf Standard Time, planned around the school's own Arabic and Islamic Education commitments, moved to post-Iftar slots in Ramadan, and arranged back to back for siblings sharing one quiet room. Scheduling is where most tuition quietly fails, so we treat it as part of the teaching.

whyPoints.title: Told plainly when nobody is free
whyPoints.description: Specialist availability is finite, particularly for minority languages and some Higher Level options. If no tutor who teaches your child's syllabus has a slot that works, we say so and give you an honest timeframe rather than offering a near-match and hoping. A wrong tutor costs more than a wait.

faqs.question: What does an ADEK inspection rating tell me about the tutoring my child needs?
faqs.answer: It tells you where the school's own capacity sits, which narrows what you should buy. The overall band is a weighted summary of a whole school, so read one level down: the judgements on students' achievement and on teaching and assessment for your child's phase and subject group. If feedback quality is criticised, an outside tutor marking your child's work to the published markscheme fills a real gap. If subject availability is the problem, no rating fixes that and an online specialist is the practical answer. Check the current report on ADEK's own site rather than an old summary.

faqs.question: Why is Al Ain inspected by ADEK rather than KHDA?
faqs.answer: Because Al Ain is part of the Emirate of Abu Dhabi, not Dubai. Private schools in Abu Dhabi, Al Ain and Al Dhafra are licensed and inspected by ADEK, the Department of Education and Knowledge. KHDA covers Dubai only, and Sharjah's private schools answer to SPEA, while the northern emirates sit with the federal Ministry of Education. This matters when you read advice online: guidance written for Dubai families about KHDA fee rules, inspection cycles or school ratings does not transfer directly to your child's school in Al Ain.

faqs.question: How much should I expect to pay per hour for a tutor in Al Ain?
faqs.answer: Market rates published by other UAE providers give the range. Budget online tuition runs from roughly AED 45 to AED 150 an hour, a qualified subject teacher online between about AED 150 and AED 300, and visiting in-home tuition from around AED 180 to AED 500 because travel is priced inside the hour. Named IB and IGCSE specialists are quoted from AED 200 to AED 450 and above. Those are other companies' figures, not ours. Compare any quote per contact hour, since monthly bundles package very different amounts of teaching.

faqs.question: Is a visiting home tutor in Al Ain worth the extra cost over online lessons?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, and it depends on the age. For primary-age children and some students with additional needs, having an adult in the room genuinely helps with focus in a way a screen does not. For Diploma and IGCSE students the calculation usually flips, because what decides the grade is whether the tutor has taught that exact paper. In a city with a smaller specialist pool, insisting on someone who can drive to your district on a Tuesday evening shrinks the list sharply. IB Gram delivers UAE tuition as live one-to-one online lessons; home visits are part of our India service only.

faqs.question: Al Ain has fewer IB schools than Abu Dhabi island. Can my child still get a Higher Level specialist?
faqs.answer: Yes, and that is the clearest reason local families use online tuition. A smaller private-school set means some Higher Level sciences and the less common languages are taught to a single small group, or are not offered at all. Online lessons remove geography from the match, so a Chemistry HL tutor who has taught the current guide can work with a student in Zakher as easily as one in Abu Dhabi. If no specialist in your child's exact syllabus has a workable slot, we will tell you that and give a realistic timeframe rather than substituting a near-match.

faqs.question: Do private tutors in the UAE need a permit, and should I ask to see one?
faqs.answer: Private tutoring in the UAE is regulated, and a permit for individual private tutors is issued through the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation. Every regulatory source we checked states that the permit itself carries no fee. Employed residents generally need their employer's agreement before tutoring privately. It is reasonable to ask any individual tutor working in the UAE about their permit position and their qualifications. Rules and processes change, so check the current requirements on the ministry's own channels rather than relying on a tutoring company's summary, including this one.

faqs.question: Which exam board does my child's school in Al Ain actually use?
faqs.answer: Check the statement of entry rather than assuming, because mixed entries are common here. Cambridge subjects carry four-digit codes such as 0580 for Mathematics, 0625 for Physics and 0620 for Chemistry. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE codes look like 4MA1, 4PH1 and 4CH1. Cambridge IGCSE 0580 also tiers into Core and Extended, and the tier caps the grade available, so it matters as much as the board. One family can easily have two children on different boards, and one student can carry both across subjects. Send us the entry document and we check it before the first session.

faqs.question: How are the marks split between the papers and the Internal Assessment in Diploma sciences?
faqs.answer: Under the current guides both Standard and Higher Level sit at 36 per cent for Paper 1, 44 per cent for Paper 2 and 20 per cent for the scientific investigation. The investigation is the component a student controls completely, in their own time, with feedback permitted, and it is worth a fifth of the grade. Families frequently buy exam cramming while that 20 per cent goes unsupervised. Weightings are revised between syllabus cycles, so confirm the current split with your school's coordinator or the published subject guide before planning around it.

faqs.question: When should a Diploma student in Al Ain start the Internal Assessment?
faqs.answer: Roughly nine months before the first paper, which for a May session means the spring and summer of DP1. The work that matters at that stage is not writing; it is narrowing the research question until the criteria are actually reachable. A question that is too broad, or that depends on data the student cannot collect, costs weeks that cannot be recovered later. Once a workable question exists, the drafting is manageable. Students who start in the autumn of DP2 collide with the Extended Essay, the TOK essay and four other investigations in the same twelve weeks.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help with the Internal Assessment without breaking the rules?
faqs.answer: Yes, within a clear line. A tutor may teach the underlying content, explain what each criterion rewards, discuss whether a research question is feasible, show the student how to mark their own draft against the descriptors, point out where a paragraph describes rather than argues, and check referencing against the school's required style. A tutor may not write or redraft any passage, supply text to insert, produce or alter data, choose the question, or write reflection entries. Any provider offering to supply a finished Internal Assessment is offering malpractice, and the consequence lands on the student.

faqs.question: Does my child still have to study Arabic and Islamic Education alongside the Diploma?
faqs.answer: In the Emirate of Abu Dhabi, ADEK requires private schools to teach Arabic, Islamic Education for Muslim students, and UAE Social Studies or moral education, for specified year groups and in specified amounts. Those hours sit on top of a six-subject Diploma or a full IGCSE set, and they carry real grade pressure on the school report even when they do not appear on the Diploma. We ask for the complete school timetable before fixing a slot, so a tuition session never collides with the school's own Arabic support. Your school's registrar can confirm exactly what applies to your child's year.

faqs.question: What is the Ministry of Education equivalency certificate, and when should we start it?
faqs.answer: It is the decision that a foreign school-leaving qualification is equivalent to the UAE national secondary certificate, which a UAE university will expect from an IB or British-curriculum applicant. For a Diploma student the usual question is whether the full Diploma was awarded and whether the subject spread meets the published threshold; for an IGCSE and A-level student it is a count of passes in a recognised combination. Start the file in DP1 or Year 11. Most problems are administrative: unattested transcripts, a name change, or a resit the school never recorded. Confirm current rules on the ministry's own portal.

faqs.question: Should my child take Maths AA or AI for UAE University admissions?
faqs.answer: Treat it as a degree decision rather than a difficulty decision, because Applications and Interpretation is not the easy option; it is the modelling and statistics route with heavy technology use and a great deal of written interpretation. Engineering, physics and some computing programmes commonly expect Analysis and Approaches, while economics, business and many life-science routes accept either. Published entry requirements change between intakes, so read the current page for the specific degree at the specific university rather than relying on what an older sibling was told. We check the route against the degree plan before a student commits.

faqs.question: Can lessons move to post-Iftar timing during Ramadan?
faqs.answer: Yes, and for most Al Ain students that is the better slot anyway. School days shorten during Ramadan and the productive hours for a teenager shift later, so we schedule lighter content work in the afternoons and move the demanding sessions to after Iftar. Because lessons are delivered online there is no travel to fit around the timing change, which is one practical advantage of the format during the month. We agree the revised timetable before Ramadan begins rather than rescheduling week by week, and go back to term timings afterwards.

faqs.question: We live in Zakher and the school run finishes late. When can sessions realistically start?
faqs.answer: Plan for a 6pm start on weekdays rather than 4.30pm. Zakher sits on the southern edge of the city towards Jebel Hafeet, and families whose children attend central or northern campuses have the longest run in Al Ain. Many Zakher families also shift the heavier subject to Friday or Saturday morning, when there is no commute at either end and a student can work for ninety minutes properly. We set the first few sessions deliberately late, see what arrival time actually looks like, then move it earlier if the family wants.

faqs.question: How does online tutoring handle practical work and the alternative-to-practical paper?
faqs.answer: The practical examination itself is run by the school or the examination centre, and no tutor replaces laboratory time. What tuition does cover is the written assessment of practical skills, which is where most of those marks actually sit: describing apparatus and method, identifying variables and controls, spotting anomalous results, handling uncertainty, and following table and graph conventions. We work through past practical and alternative-to-practical papers on screen, annotating the student's answers against the published markscheme. For the Diploma investigation, the design and analysis work is exactly what online sessions suit.

faqs.question: What happens if the first tutor is not the right match for my child?
faqs.answer: Tell us after the first or second session and we change the tutor, not the plan. A mismatch is usually about pace or explanation style rather than competence, and it shows up quickly: a student who answers in single words, or who leaves a session without a clear next task. We would rather re-match in week two than discover in week ten that nothing moved. The diagnostic session exists partly for this reason, because it gives both the tutor and the parent something concrete to judge the fit against.

faqs.question: Is it too late to start if the first paper is six weeks away?
faqs.answer: It is late for content and useful for technique. Six weeks before a paper, teaching new topics rarely pays; marking timed papers does. A short block in that window works when it is built around whole past papers, marked to the published markscheme, with errors logged by type rather than by topic, so the student keeps meeting the same mistake until it stops. What a six-week block cannot do is close a year-wide content gap, and we will say so plainly rather than selling a package that cannot deliver. No tutor can promise a particular score.

al-ain.closingHeading: Start with the report, then choose the subject specialist
al-ain.closingBody: Send us the last school report, the ADEK inspection page for your child's phase if you have it, and the statement of entry. We will read them, tell you whether the gap is content, technique, coursework or scheduling, and match an online IB tutor in Al Ain who teaches that exact syllabus. The first session is a marked paper, not a sales call, and if the honest answer is that your child does not need weekly tuition, that is what you will hear. Lessons are live one-to-one video, booked in Gulf Standard Time, with written feedback you can read.

Families searching for IB and IGCSE tutors in Al Jimi are frequently solving an availability problem: a Higher Level subject not offered, an option block that collides, a cohort of five. This page covers what a small school can timetable, Higher against Standard Level dimension by dimension, and the private candidate route. Lessons are one-to-one over live video.

al-ain/al-jimi.tutorsIntro: The tutors below are matched to subjects rather than to a city, which is the point of the format. A Higher Level Chemistry specialist does not have to live in Al Ain to teach a student in Al Jimi, and in practice there are considerably more of them elsewhere.

intro.heading: In a small school, the gap is often a whole subject
paragraphs: Al Jimi sits in the central-western part of Al Ain, around the mall and the oasis, with Al Qattara, Al Mutawaa and Al Muwaiji adjoining it. Al Ain itself is part of the Abu Dhabi emirate and therefore regulated by the Department of Education and Knowledge, 130 kilometres inland from the capital, and its private-school set is substantially smaller than the island's. That single structural fact changes what tutoring is for here.

In a large city school the gap a tutor fills is usually narrow: a topic that did not land, a technique that was never corrected, a coursework draft nobody read twice. In a smaller school the gap is often categorical. The Higher Level subject your child wants may not run, because a viable set needs a minimum number of students and the cohort is thin. An option block may place two subjects your child needs in the same column. A subject may run with five students and a teacher covering it alongside two others. None of those is a failing on the school's part; they are arithmetic.

What that produces is a different set of parental questions from the ones competitor pages answer. Not how do I find a maths tutor, but can my child take Higher Level Physics at all, and if not, what are the options. Not how much does tuition cost, but what does it mean to study a subject the school does not teach. Not is online as good as in person, but is there anybody in Al Ain who teaches this subject, and if not, does that matter.

The honest answer to the last of those is that it does not matter much, because the format removes the geography. A Higher Level Economics specialist teaching from anywhere in the time zone is available to a student in Al Jimi in exactly the way a locally resident generalist is, and there are considerably more of the former. The 130 kilometres is a constraint on who can arrive at a door and no constraint at all on who can teach on a screen.

There is a timing point that runs through all of it and deserves saying on its own. Every response to an availability problem requires notice. Moving a subject between option blocks, finding a centre that will enter an external candidate, teaching a two-year course from outside the school, changing school: each of those is possible in November of Year 11 and impossible in June of Year 12. The families who come out of this well are not the ones with the most money. They are the ones who asked for the timetable a year early.

So this page sets out what Al Ain schools typically can and cannot timetable, compares Higher and Standard Level properly across seven dimensions rather than in a sentence, explains the private candidate route for a subject the school cannot offer, and says plainly what self-teaching a subject actually requires. Lessons are delivered one-to-one over live video, and that is also the practical reason any of this is possible from here rather than a matter of preference.

al-ain/al-jimi.programmesIntro: The notes below are written around availability, because in a smaller school set the question of whether a course runs at all comes before any question about how it is taught.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects, three at Higher Level and three at Standard, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS. The structure is the constraint in a small school: a student must find three Higher Level courses that actually run and that do not collide in the option blocks, which narrows real choice considerably.
programmes.countryNote: Al Ain Diploma cohorts are small, which has genuine advantages, more teacher attention and a closer group, and one serious disadvantage. If the Higher Level subject your child needs for a university course does not run, the decision has to be made in Year 11 rather than discovered in Year 12. Ask the school for its option blocks a full year ahead.

programmes.name: IGCSE
programmes.description: Cambridge International and Pearson Edexcel both operate here, with Cambridge tiering several subjects into Core and Extended and capping Core at grade C. IGCSE option lists are usually wider than Diploma ones because the cohort is larger and the teaching load per subject is lower.
programmes.countryNote: The practical Al Ain issue at IGCSE is the less common subjects: a second science, a specific language, computer science or a creative subject may not run at all. The subject your child drops at fourteen can close a Higher Level door at sixteen, which is why the Year 9 options conversation matters more here than in a larger city.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups marked against four lettered criteria, each out of eight, with process assessed alongside content. In a small school the same teacher often carries a subject across several year groups, which means consistency is good and specialist depth at the top end can be thinner.
programmes.countryNote: For an Al Ain family the MYP matters mainly as preparation for a narrow Diploma choice. A student who keeps a second science and a language going through MYP preserves options that a thin Diploma option block will otherwise close for them two years later.

programmes.name: A Level
programmes.description: Linear qualifications with all assessment at the end and little coursework in most subjects. Three or four subjects studied deeply, which in a small school can be easier to timetable than a full Diploma because there are fewer courses to staff.
programmes.countryNote: Where a Diploma option block cannot accommodate a student's needs, A Level is sometimes the better route in Al Ain simply because it requires fewer simultaneous courses. It also satisfies the Ministry of Education's British track, which asks for one accredited A Level at grade E or better, or two AS Levels at the same grade, alongside five IGCSE or GCSE subjects at no less than E or grade 3.

al-ain/al-jimi.subjectsIntro: The notes below say something about availability as well as content, because in Al Ain the first question about a subject is often whether anybody nearby teaches it at all.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Papers 1 and 2 carry 36% and 44% in the Diploma with the investigation at 20%. Higher Level organic mechanisms and energetics are the most frequently requested gap from Al Ain, partly because Higher Level sets here are small and partly because the material needs hand-drawn repetition.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Higher Level Physics is one of the courses most likely not to run in a small school, because the cohort rarely reaches a viable size. Where it does run, fields and the Higher Level extension topics are the standard loss points.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Usually available because demand is higher. Built on unifying themes at Diploma level with heavy unseen-context questioning, where students lose marks describing a trend when the command term asked them to explain a cause.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Standard Level sits two papers at 40% each with a 20% exploration; Higher Level adds Paper 3 at 20%. Higher Level Analysis and Approaches is frequently the single hardest course to staff in a small school and the one most often requested from outside.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Modelling and statistics with the graphic display calculator throughout. More commonly offered in smaller schools than Analysis and Approaches because it suits a broader cohort, which makes the route choice partly an availability question rather than purely a preference.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Standard Level is Paper 1 at 30%, Paper 2 at 40% and the portfolio at 30%, with a quantitative Paper 3 added at Higher Level. Higher Level Economics is a common gap in smaller schools and a subject several UAE university routes expect.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Higher Level sits Paper 1 at 35% and Paper 2 at 40% with the project at 25%. The project needs real organisational access, and in a small cohort students often choose the same two or three local businesses, which produces generic analysis.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Unseen analysis, comparative essay, and the Individual Oral at 30% of Standard Level, with the HL essay at 20% added at Higher Level. Reliably available, and the loss point is summarising a text rather than analysing the writer's choices.

subjects.name: Computer Science
subjects.description: One of the least likely subjects to run at Higher Level in a smaller school, and increasingly requested. It is also one of the thinner subjects in the regional tutor pool, so it is worth asking about a long way in advance.

subjects.name: Arabic as a first and additional language
subjects.description: Mandatory alongside the international programme under the federal rules, with separate provision and different expectations for Arab and non-Arab students. Arabic A at Diploma level is better served in Al Ain than many other subjects.

subjects.name: Psychology
subjects.description: A frequent Diploma choice that smaller schools often cannot staff, and one where students underestimate the research-methods component. The internal assessment is an experimental replication with strict ethical constraints that trip up the unprepared.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge
subjects.description: A 1,600-word essay on a prescribed title plus the exhibition with its 950-word commentary. In a small school it is often taught by a teacher carrying it alongside a full subject load, so it is the component most likely to be under-supported.

al-ain/al-jimi.regionsIntro: Al Ain is a compact, low-rise city, so these districts are all within a short drive of Al Jimi and the school choice is made across them.

regions.name: Al Muwaiji
regions.note: Immediately west of Al Jimi, residential and largely Emirati, with the historic fort at its centre. Short school runs in both directions, and households here face the same thin Diploma option lists.

regions.name: Al Towayya
regions.note: North-east towards Tawam, with the hospital and medical community nearby. A significant number of families here work shifts, which shapes when tutoring can happen in a way it does not elsewhere in the city.

regions.name: Al Khabisi
regions.note: East of Al Jimi, with established school provision including some of the city's longest-standing private schools. One of the main school destinations for Al Jimi families.

regions.name: Hili
regions.note: North of the city centre, residential with the archaeological park nearby. Reachable within a few minutes, and part of the same small set of school options.

regions.name: Al Maqam
regions.note: South-east, where the UAE University campus sits. Relevant academically because it shapes what local families aim at and which subject prerequisites matter for their applications.

regions.name: Zakher
regions.note: South of the city on the way towards the Omani border, residential and spread out. Longer runs into the central school cluster, which pushes tutoring towards weekends for these households.

regions.name: Falaj Hazza
regions.note: West towards the Jebel Hafeet side, residential with local provision. Another district drawing on the same central school cluster, with the same Higher Level availability constraints.
